questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The region marked corresponds to the surface marking for which of the following structures:
questions.explanation:
The region marked corresponds to the surface marking for the right atrium.

The costal margin, xiphoid process, and the mid-clavicular line are seen in this image. The examiner draws a laterally convex line that extends from a level below the 2nd costal cartilage (as clued in by the sternal angle) i.e., 3rd costal cartilage to about 3 spaces below i.e., the 6th costal cartilage. This line is about 1.2 cms lateral to the sternal edge. These suggest that the region marked corresponds to the surface marking for the right atrium.

The projection of the cardiac borders, of an average adult, onto the anterior thoracic wall forms a trapezoid.  This can be mapped out using the percussion method by looking for cardiac dullness. 

The varying heart borders and the corresponding surface markings are as follows:

  • Upper border: Slopes gently from the second left costal cartilage to the third right costal cartilage. It corresponds to the left atrium.
  • Right border: Convex to the right and runs from the third to the sixth right costal cartilages, 1–2 cm lateral to the sternal edge. It corresponds to the right atrium.
  • Inferior border or acute border: Runs leftwards from the 6th right costal cartilage to the cardiac apex which is located approximately 9 cm lateral to the midline, often in the left 5th intercostal space or level with the 5th or 6th rib. It corresponds to the right ventricle.
  • Left border or obtuse border: Convex laterally on the left. It extends superomedially from the cardiac apex to meet the second left costal cartilage about 1 cm from the left sternal edge. It corresponds to the left ventricle.

questions.question: Marked structure is derived from the______

The structure marked is the membranous part of the interventricular septum. It is derived from endocardial cushions.

Endocardial cushions are soft tissue masses that protrude in the atrioventricular and conotruncal regions. 

  • Atrioventricular cushions are derived from overlying endocardial cells.
  • The conotruncal cushions are derived from the neural crest cells.

  • Atrioventricular canals
  • Atrioventricular valves
  • Aortic and pulmonary channels

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the structure(s) in the following histological image.
questions.explanation:
The above histology image shows the glomerulus.

Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium. Blood enters the tuft through an afferent arteriole and leaves it through an efferent arteriole. It is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix.

The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes.

The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus.



Option A: Leydig cells, also known as interstitial cells of Leydig, are present in the interstitial connective between seminiferous tubules.

The testis contains numerous seminiferous tubules separated by connective tissue in between. Seminiferous tubules are lined by several spermatogonia cells, which produce spermatozoa, and Sertoli (sustentacular) cells, which have a supportive function. 

The connective tissue in between the tubules is made up of Leydig cells, collagen fibers, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, blood vessels, and lymphatics. Leydig cells are large, round, or polyhedral cells with eccentric nuclei. They are lightly stained and often have a foamy appearance. They secrete testosterone upon stimulation by luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary.

The image below shows seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells.



Option B: Islets of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers and contain numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. The islet cells are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The islet of Langerhans is mainly composed of three types of cells:

  • α or A cells - located peripherally and secrete glucagon 
  • β or B cells - located centrally and produce insulin 
  • δ or D cells - scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin

The image given below shows the islets of Langerhans.



Option C: Hassall's corpuscles are small rounded structures present in the medulla of the thymus. Each corpuscle has a central core of degenerated epithelial cells and macrophages surrounded by concentrically arranged epithelial cells. The degenerated cells ultimately give pink staining hyaline mass. The function of the corpuscles of Hassall is still not known.

The image given below shows Hassall's corpuscle.

questions.question: Injury at which of the following marked sites causes failure of dorsiflexion?
questions.explanation:
The site marked as '3' in the x-ray given above is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also know as common peroneal nerve)

The common fibular nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

  Superficial fibular nerve Deep fibular nerve
Motor innervation
  • Peroneus longus
  • Peroneus brevis
  • Extensor digitorum longus
  • Extensor hallucis longus
  • Tibialis anterior
  • Peroneus tertius
Sensory innervation
  • Lateral aspect of the lower leg
  • Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital web-space

 
  • The first interdigital space
 

 



Injury to the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve) at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A defect in which of the following aortic arches causes the defect shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
The image above shows a patent ductus arteriosus due to a defect in the left side of the 6th aortic arch.

Usually, in term infants, the ductus arteriosus closes within 72 hours of birth. Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

PDA usually presents with a hyperdynamic precordium, bounding peripheral pulses, wide pulse pressure, a machine-like continuous or systolic murmur, cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, hepatomegaly, increasing oxygen dependence, carbon dioxide retention, and renal failure.

In a majority of cases, PDA closes spontaneously. If spontaneous closure fails to occur, COX inhibitors like indomethacin or ibuprofen can be used. Surgical ligation is indicated in case of contraindications to medical management or failure of the same.

Other options

Option A: The 4th right aortic arch gives rise to the proximal part of the right subclavian artery. 

Option B: The 4th left aortic arch gives rise to the arch of the aorta. Defects involving the 4th left aortic arch could cause a variety of aortic arch anomalies, such as interruption of the aortic arch, but not PDA.

Option C: The 6th right aortic arch forms the proximal part of the right pulmonary artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with swelling under the left ear lobule and complains of pain. Which of the following structures is the likely cause of the pain?
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
questions.explanation:
The cause of the pain in this patient complaining of pain in the parotid region is likely to be the greater auricular nerve.

The greater auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the parotid gland and the ear lobule. Pain associated with swelling and inflammation in the parotid region could be transmitted through the greater auricular nerve. The parotid gland is covered by a parotid capsule that is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Any acute inflammation of the gland such as acute sialadenitis results in pain in the pre­auricular region. The pain is mainly due to stretching of the capsule resulting in stimulation of the greater auricular nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The facial nerve is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling. The Hitzelberger sign(numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall of the external auditory canal), associated with facial nerve involvement, is seen in acoustic neuroma and is not the cause of pain in this scenario. 

Option D: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is not the correct answer because the investing layer of deep cervical fascia itself does not transmit pain sensation. The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is a layer of connective tissue that envelops the neck and extends to cover the parotid gland, forming the parotid capsule. While inflammation or swelling in the parotid gland can stretch the capsule and cause pain, the actual transmission of pain sensation is mediated by sensory nerves, such as the greater auricular nerve, which innervates the skin over the parotid gland and the ear lobule.

The greater auricular nerve (Option B) is a more appropriate answer in this context, as it is responsible for carrying the pain sensation from the area of swelling and inflammation in the parotid region.

Option C: The auriculotemporal nerve can cause referred pain due to caries tooth, ulcerative lesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia. However, it is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 6-month-old boy was brought to the casualty with seizures. The pediatrician tries to do CSF sampling. What are the structures punctured by the pediatrician while piercing through the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows the skull of an infant and the arrow points towards the anterior fontanelle. The procedure of collecting CSF from the anterior fontanelle is called ventricular tapping. The various structures pierced are the scalp, dura, and arachnoid.

Fontanelle tap/ Percutaneous ventricular puncture:

A fontanelle tap or percutaneous ventricular puncture is performed in infants without access to a VP shunt, who require urgent ventricular decompression and have an open anterior fontanelle. The infants’ open fontanelle is directly punctured with a butterfly needle to enter the lateral ventricle to collect CSF samples or release the pressure or place a drain/catheter. 

A 25-gauge butterfly needle is inserted through the anterolateral aspect of the anterior fontanelle (away from the midline, avoiding the superior sagittal sinus).

The image below shows the various fontanelles.

 



 

The scalp is a soft tissue that covers the calvaria of the skull. It consists of five layers (Mnemonic: SCALP). Below the scalp and the calvaria lie the meningeal layers, namely, pachymeninges [arachnoid + dura mater (P-AD)] and leptomeninges [arachnoid + pia mater (L-AP)]. One must reach the subarachnoid space below the arachnoid layer to collect or tap CSF. So, the layers pierced in the order are as follows:

  1. Skin
  2. Connective tissue (superficial fascia) with blood vessels and nerves
  3. Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) with occipitofrontalis muscle
  4. Loose areolar (subaponeurotic) tissue
  5. Pericranium
  6. Dura mater
  7. Arachnoid membrane

The given images show the various layers that are pierced.

The given image is a cadaveric specimen with the arrow pointing towards, the tonsillar fossa, and the given clinical vignette is suggestive of tonsillitis. Post tonsillectomy hemorrhage is commonly venous in origin, from the paratonsillar/ external palatine vein. 

Torrential hemorrhage can be due to injury to an aberrantly large or aberrantly placed tonsillar arterial branch of the facial artery.

Blood supply of the tonsils: 

Arterial supply:

  • The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the main supply.
  • Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery.
  • Ascending pharyngeal branch of the external carotid artery.
  • Dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery.
  • Descending palatine branches of the maxillary artery.

Venous supply:

  • Veins from the tonsils drain into paratonsillar vein which joins the common facial vein and pharyngeal venous plexus.

Types of Hemorrhage seen during/post tonsillectomy:

  • Primary hemorrhage:
    • Occurs during surgery due to injury to blood vessels.
    • Can be controlled by pressure, ligation, or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.
  • Reactionary hemorrhage:
    • It occurs within 24 hours of surgery.
    • It may be due to dislodgement of the clot, slippage of ligature, or return of blood pressure to normal.
    • It is managed by removal of clot and application of pressure or vasoconstrictor.
    • If not controlled the patient is anesthetized and hemorrhage is managed by re-exploration.
  • Secondary hemorrhage:
    • It occurs between 24 hours to 10 days (most common between 5th to 8th postoperative days).
    • It is due to sepsis and premature separation of the membrane.
    • The patient is started on IV antibiotics and if not controlled, general anesthesia is given and the bleeding vessel is electrocoagulated or ligated.

A medially placed column of cells innervates the contralateral superior rectus.

Red Nucleus/ Nucleus Ruber

It is a rounded mass of grey matter located dorsomedial to the substantial nigra. It has a reddish hue in fresh specimens due to its extensive vascularity and the presence of ferric iron pigments in multipolar neurons.

questions.question: Fibers from the marked structure terminate at which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The peduncle highlighted in the image is the superior cerebellar peduncle. The superior cerebellar peduncle includes fibers from deep cerebellar nuclei that project to the brainstem, red nucleus, and thalamus. It also contains the ventral spinocerebellar tract fibers.

The superior cerebellar peduncle contains all the efferent fibers from the dentate, emboliform, and the globose nuclei, and a small fascicle from the fastigial nucleus. Its fibers decussate in the caudal mesencephalon and are destined to synapse in the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. The middle cerebellar peduncle contains only afferent fibers from the contralateral pontine nuclei. The inferior cerebellar peduncle is a mixture of afferent fibers from the brainstem and spinal cord and efferent fibers to the vestibular nuclei.

The image below summarizes the various tracts in the cerebellar unit.



The cerebellum consists of two hemispheres (right and left) joined by a median vermis. It is divided into three lobes:-

  • Anterior lobe - lies superiorly above the primary fissure
  • Middle lobe - lies inferiorly below the primary fissure. It is the largest lobe. It is also called the posterior lobe.
  • Flocculonodular lobe - lies posterior to the uvulonodular fissure

It has two surfaces - superior and inferior separated by a horizontal fissure. It is connected to the other parts of the central nervous system via three peduncles

  • Superior cerebellar peduncle -connecting to the midbrain
  • Middle cerebellar peduncle - connecting to the pons
  • Inferior cerebellar peduncle - connecting to the medulla oblongata

questions.question: A woman with right-sided loss of sensations of both the upper and lower limb complains of shooting pain from her fingers to the right shoulder and a burning sensation when touching cold water. The given clinical stem of a hemi-sensory loss and severe excruciating pain of the affected areas is suggestive of thalamic pain syndrome also known as Dejerine Roussy syndrome. Hence, thalamus marked as B is most likely to be involved.

Occlusion of these thalamic and thalamogeniculate branches results in the thalamic pain syndrome. It is characterized by C/L hemisensory loss which starts as numbness and progresses to cause severe burning pain in the affected regions. As the thalamus is the site for the relay of sensory information between the periphery and cortex, a lesion in the thalamus causes a miscommunication between the afferent pathway and cortex of the brain. Pain occurs during the recovery from the thalamic infarct. This pain responds poorly to analgesics. Anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine or gabapentin or tricyclic antidepressants may be beneficial.

questions.question: A 25-year-old male presented with symptoms of inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits. He was also not able to hold a piece of paper between his fingers. What is the likely site of injury?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical situation with a positive card test and an inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits, suggests an ulnar nerve injury. The most likely site of injury would thus be medial epicondyle: site C

Injury at the medial epicondyle damages the ulnar nerve, leading to paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris (loss of ulnar deviation) and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (loss of distal interphalangeal joint flexion). It leads to hypothenar paralysis (lead to atrophy) and sensory loss. Also, flexor digitorum superficialis (supplied by median nerve) and extensor digitorum (supplied by the radial nerve) are still functional. Hence complete paralysis of the 3rd and 4th digits is not seen.  The positive card test is due to the weakness of palmar interossei leading to loss of adduction.

Ulnar nerve branches and supply: 

Superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis, skin on the palmar surface of medial 1½ fingers. The deep branch runs within the concavity of deep palmar arch and supplies all intrinsic muscles of the hand (except first 2 lumbricals and thenar muscles).

Upper (superior) lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (Option-C) that innervates the skin over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area). Thus, this is not the best of the given four options.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A boy with a history of a fall from a tree presents with a lurching gait and dragging of his feet. Which of the following structures are involved?
questions.explanation:
The structure involved in causing lurching gait in the child is gluteus medius (marked as 2).

The gluteus medius originates from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines. Insertion of the muscle is at the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

Gluteus medius and minimus are powerful abductors of the hip joint. Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus:

  • When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, on the opposite supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in a slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.
  • The actions of these muscles are affected when there is an injury to the superior gluteal nerve, neck of the femur, or loss of normal angulation of the shaft of the femur. This occurs in conditions like paralysis of the glutei, developmental dysplasia of the hip, etc.
  • When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis sinks down on the unsupported (normal) side, when the patient tries to stand on the affected limb. This leads to a positive Trendelenburg's sign with a characteristic lurching gait - the patient lurches towards the affected side with contralateral pelvis drop. 


Other options

1 - Gluteus maximus - involved in the extension of flexed thigh, abduction (only upper fibres), and lateral rotation at the hip joint. Insertion is at the iliotibial tract. 

3 - Piriformis - involved in lateral rotation and assists abduction at the hip joint. It is inserted into the medial side of greater trochanter of the femur. Entrapment of the sciatic nerve in the piriformis can lead to piriformis syndrome.

4 - Sciatic nerve - The nerve passes over the obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior and quadratus femoris. It supplies knee flexors and muscles below the knee. Paralysis of this nerve results in flail foot and severe difficulty in walking.

questions.question: A patient after a road traffic accident presents to the emergency room with difficulty in swallowing and slurred speech. Investigations reveal fractures in the occipitotemporal region. Which of the following areas should be tested in order to find the nerve which is involved?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of the involvement of 9th and 10th cranial nerves due to occipitotemporal fracture and they are examined by testing the uvula which is marked as 2 in the given image.

The jugular foramen is located between the lower border of the petrous part of the temporal bone and the condylar part of the occipital bone. As the investigations reveal fractures in the occipitotemporal region, along with the history of difficulty in swallowing and slurred speech, are suggestive of injury to the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve passing through the jugular foramen.

Unilateral lesions of IX and X cranial nerves are commonly caused by skull-base fractures, strokes, or tumors.

Glossopharyngeal and Vagus nerve examination include:

  • Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula(marked as 2 in the given image) at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
  • The pharyngeal (“gag”) reflex is evaluated by stimulating the posterior pharyngeal wall on each side with a sterile, blunt object (e.g., tongue blade)

Patients with a proximal unilateral lesion of the vagus nerve complain of dysphagia. There will be a weakness of the soft palate muscles on the affected side. Attempts to voluntarily elevate the soft palate, like by asking the patient to say “aah” will reveal a weakness in elevation of the palate on the affected side. Along with this, there will be deviation of the uvula to the normal side, due to the unopposed action of palatal muscles on that side.

questions.question: The cell marked in the below slide is inhibitory to
questions.explanation:
The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell. It is inhibitory to deep cerebellar nuclei.  

Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum. They are evenly spaced and arranged in a single layer between molecular and granular cell layers. The dendrite from each cell passes upward to enter the molecular layer and the axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer, and terminates on the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex. They receive excitatory input from the climbing fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus and mossy fibers. 

Pathological significance of Purkinje cells:

  • Negri bodies in rabies are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum.
  • In paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells due to antibodies directed against them. 
  • Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of the hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The marked structure develops from which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
The structure marked in the given image is the azygos vein, which develops from the supracardinal vein.

The azygos system of veins forms a connecting channel between the superior and inferior venae cavae. It occupies the upper part of the posterior abdominal wall and the posterior mediastinum. It also connects the portal, caval system, and vertebral venous systems.It drains the thoracic wall and the upper lumbar region.

Development: The azygos venous system arises from the supra cardinal veins embryologically. The right supra cardinal vein becomes the azygos vein, while the left supra cardinal vein becomes the hemiazygos vein.

  • The 4th to 11th right intercostal veins empty into the right supracardinal vein, which together with a portion of the posterior cardinal vein forms the azygos vein.
  • On the left, the 4th to 7th intercostal veins enter into the left supracardinal vein, and the left supracardinal vein, then known as the hemiazygos vein, which also empties into the azygos vein.

Other options: Cardinal veins form the main venous drainage system of the embryo. It consists of,

  • Anterior cardinal veins, which drain the cephalic part of the embryo, and
  • Posterior cardinal veins, which drain the rest of the embryo.

During the fifth to the seventh weeks, a number of additional veins are formed. It includes,

  • Subcardinal veins, which mainly drain the kidneys;
  • Sacrocardinal veins, which drain the lower extremities;
  • Supracardinal veins, which drain the body wall by way of the intercostal veins.

Below image shows cardinal veins development.

questions.question:
Inferior thyroid artery supplies which of the following structures?
  1. Thyroid
  2. Parathyroid
  3. Esophagus
  4. Thymus
questions.explanation:
All the given 4 structures are supplied by the Inferior thyroid artery.

Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, which in turn, is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. The inferior thyroid artery loops upwards anterior to the medial border of the scalenus anterior, turns medially just below the sixth cervical transverse process, and then descends on longus colli to the lower border of the thyroid gland.

Branches:

  • Pharyngeal branches: These supply the lower part of the pharynx.
    • Tracheal branches supply the trachea and anastomose with the bronchial arteries;
    • Oesophageal branches supply the oesophagus and anastomose with the oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta; and
    • Inferior and ascending glandular branches supply the posterior and inferior regions of the thyroid gland, and anastomose with the contralateral inferior and ipsilateral superior thyroid arteries.
    • The ascending branch also supplies the parathyroid glands.
  • Ascending cervical artery
  • Inferior laryngeal
  • Muscular branches

Note: Thymic branches originating from the internal thoracic, inferior thyroid artery, and sometimes superior thyroid arteries supply the thymus and the surrounding mediastinal connective tissue.

questions.question: Which part of this bone is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa?
questions.explanation:
The part of the scapula marked as 1 is the coracoid process and it is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa. The tip of the coracoid process lies approximately 2.5 cm below the clavicle, immediately lateral to the infraclavicular fossa (deltopectoral triangle). Hence, the coracoid process can be palpated below the clavicle.

The coracoid process arises from the upper border of the neck of the scapula and it projects forwards and slightly laterally. Attachments at the coracoid process include 

  • The conoid portion of the coracoclavicular ligament 
  • Pectoralis minor 
  • Medial end of coraco-acromial ligament
  • Coracohumeral ligament 
  • Glenocorocoid ligament 
  • Coracobrachialis muscle

Other options 

Option B - Acromian process continues from the spine of the scapula. The acromion is subcutaneous over its dorsal surface, The attachments at the acromion are the coracoacromial ligament, the articular capsule of the acromioclavicular joint, and horizontal fibers of the trapezius. 

Option C - The glenoid fossa is present at the lateral angle of the scapula. It is articular with the humerus to form the shoulder joint. 

Option D - The inferior angle lies over the seventh rib. Dorsally, it is related to latissimus dorsi. The angle is visible when the arm is raised over the head.

questions.question: Identify the pelvic diaphragm in the picture given below.
questions.explanation:
The structure marked "1" is the levator ani muscle which is part of the pelvic diaphragm.

Other structures marked in the above image are

2: External anal sphincter

3: Internal anal sphincter

4: Pudendal canal

Pelvic diaphragm 

The muscular part of the pelvic floor is the pelvic diaphragm. It is attached to the pelvic wall on either side between the greater and lesser sciatic foramen. Levator ani and coccygeus muscles form the pelvic diaphragm and delineate the lower limit of the true pelvis. 

Levator ani is formed by pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, and puborectalis. The muscles blend together posterior to the vagina in women and around the anus in both sexes. Posterior to the anal aperture, the form the anococcygeal body attaches to the coccyx. Urogenital hiatus is present anteriorly separating the muscles. This allows the urethra and vagina to pass through. Levator ani reinforces the external anal sphincter. In women, it functions as the vaginal sphincter. 

The coccygeus muscles, one on each side are triangular in shape and form the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm. The apices are attached to the tips of ischial spines. The bases are attached to the coccyx and sacrum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Third part of vertebral artery is related to which of the following ?
questions.explanation:
The third part of the vertebral artery (V3) is related to the area marked 2, which is the posterior arch of the first cervical vertebra or the atlas.

The given image shows the first cervical vertebra - atlas.

  • The area marked 1 is the posterior tubercle.
  • The area marked 2 is the posterior arch. The superior surface bears a groove for the of vertebral artery and venous plexus immediately behind.
  • The area marked 3 is the superior articular facet.
  • The area marked 4 is the posterior surface of the anterior arch. It gives attachment to the apex of dens from the second cervical vertebra. 

The vertebral artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It passes through the foramina of transverse processes of C6 to C1 cervical vertebrae and enters the cranium through the foramen magnum. The vertebral arteries of both sides join to form the basilar artery. In its course, it is divided into four parts:

The first part, V1, begins at its origin from the subclavian artery and ends at its entry into the transverse process of the C6 cervical vertebra. This part is crossed by the inferior thyroid artery on both sides, and thoracic duct on the left side, and the right lymphatic duct on the right side. 

The second part, V2 is that part of the artery ascending through the foramina in the transverse process of the cervical vertebrae. 

The third part, V3 is curved backward behind the atlas. In this position, it lies in a groove on the posterior arch of the atlas. This part of the artery lies in the suboccipital triangle. 

The fourth part, V4 pierces the dura and arachnoid mater and unites with the contralateral vertebral artery to form the midline basilar artery at the lower border of pons.

questions.question: What is the most common complication of the central line insertion below the marked bone?
questions.explanation:
The bone marked in the above image is the left clavicle. The most common complication of a central line insertion below this bone is an arterial puncture.

Complications of central vein catheterization are

  • Arterial puncture- this is the most common complication. 
  • Cardiac tamponade is the most important life-threatening complication. It occurs as a result of puncture of intrapericardial superior vena cava, right atrium, or right ventricle.
  • Pneumothorax- injury to the underlying pleura may lead to pneumothorax. This is more common in subclavian vein catheterization.
  • Chylothorax can occur particularly in left subclavian vein catheterisation. But it is not the most common.
  • Injury to the associated nerves like brachial plexus, stellate ganglion, phrenic nerve, or vocal cords.
  • Thromboembolism leading to venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism is more common with femoral veins.
  • Infections

Central venous catheterization is the insertion of the catheter into a large central vein. The veins preferred largely depend on the underlying disease in the patient, the clinical setting, and the expertise of the doctor. 

The internal jugular vein is preferred when the patient has:

  • Bleeding diathesis- Bleeding from this vein can be easily detected and can be controlled with pressure. 
  • Pneumothorax- The lesser risk of injury to the lung
  • Needs cardiac pacing- right internal jugular vein is used.

Femoral or subclavian veins can be used in patients when the neck is immobilized using a cervical collar.

questions.question: Identify the cranial nerve passing through the given structure
questions.explanation:
In the given image, the dorsal aspect of the brainstem is marked and the cranial nerve that is passing there is the trochlear nerve (CN IV). 

The trochlear nerve is the fourth cranial nerve that originates from the trochlear nuclei within the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. It is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal surface of the brainstem and has the longest intracranial course. It passes on to the lateral surface of the crus of cerebellar peduncle and lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. The nerve then crosses the oculomotor nerve to enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure to exclusively supply the contralateral superior oblique muscle.

The main actions of superior oblique are

  • Depression in adducted position- The muscle elevates the posterior of the eye causing the front of the eye to be depressed. Patients with trochlear nerve palsy have difficulty in looking downwards when eyes are in the adducted position. 
  • Abduction
  • Intortion of the eyeball.

Other options- Oculomotor (CN III), trigeminal (CN V) and abducens (CN VI) nerves exit ventrally from the brainstem.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presented with vision loss. On radiological investigation, an aneurysm causing damage to the optic chiasma was noted. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be the artery that is causing the damage?
questions.explanation:
An aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery is most likely to be causing damage to the optic chiasma, leading to vision loss in this patient.

Circle of Willis is a large arterial anastomosis that unites the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. It lies in the subarachnoid space within the basal cisterns that surround the optic chiasma and infundibulum.

Anterior communicating artery aneurysm: 

Anterior communicating artery (Acom) links the right and left anterior cerebral arteries and is directed anterior and superior to the optic chiasma. The aneurysm will protrude in the posterior direction and will impinge upon the optic chiasma from above, leading to loss of vision.

Compression of the optic chiasma (central lesion) by an ACom aneurysm, will lead to bitemporal hemianopia i.e, loss of vision in the left/temporal halves of both visual fields. Nasal fibers of each retina cross through the chiasma at this level and hence, these fibers will be compromised.

In the case of a bilateral peripheral lesion of the optic chiasma, binasal hemianopia will be seen.

Other causes of chiasmal lesions are

  • Pituitary adenoma (most common)
  • Craniopharyngioma
  • Meningioma
  • Glioma

Blood supply of optic chiasma: The left and right anterior cerebral arteries, along with the superior hypophyseal artery (branch of the internal carotid artery) form the blood supply of optic chiasma.



 

The given cadaveric image below is of the vascular structures (Circle of Willis) at the base of the brain.



 

Investigation: Digital subtraction angiogram is the definitive imaging modality for aneurysms arising from the circle of Willis. Other investigations are CT and MRI.

Other options:

Aneurysms of the anterior choroidal artery (option B) and middle cerebral artery (option C) aneurysms will not compress the optic chiasma as they are anatomically not in close proximity to be able to exert pressure on the chiasma and cause loss of vision.

Despite the anatomical proximity of the anterior cerebral artery (option D) to the optic chiasma, anterior communicating artery (Acom) aneurysm is the commonest intracranial aneurysm.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man presented with fever and massive splenomegaly. On palpation, the spleen was 15 cm and directed obliquely when measured from the right iliac fossa. Which of the following structures prevent the vertical and downward descent of the spleen?
questions.explanation:
The vertical and downward descent of the spleen is prevented by the phrenicocolic ligament.

The phrenicocolic ligament is not attached to the spleen. It attaches the splenic flexure of the colon to the diaphragm. 

When the spleen gets enlarged, the phrenicocolic ligament along with the splenic flexure of the colon restricts its downward displacement. The enlargement of the spleen occurs towards the right iliac fossa and hence the spleen is directed obliquely.

Splenic ligaments and their attachments:

Splenic ligament Attachments  Contents
Phrenicocolic ligament Diaphragm to the splenic flexure of the colon -
Phrenicosplenic ligament The undersurface of the diaphragm to the spleen -
Splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament Hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney Tail of pancreas
Splenic artery and vein
Gastrosplenic ligament The greater curvature of the stomach to the upper pole of the spleen Short gastric vessels
Left gastroepiploic artery


 

Cross-sectional view of the spleen and its ligaments



 

The spleen becomes palpable when it is enlarged 2-3 times more than its normal size. A characteristic splenic notch can be felt in the medial border in an enlarged spleen. Also, fingers cannot be insinuated between the left costal margin and the enlarged spleen.

In the classical method of palpation, the right hand (with fingers pointed towards the left costal margin) is placed on the right iliac fossa. Palpation begins from the right iliac fossa towards the left hypochondrium in an upwards and lateral direction. Between each breath of the patient, the edge of the spleen can be felt.

In the hooking method, the hooked fingers of the right hand are placed under the left costal margin, and with the left hand, pressure is exerted over the posterolateral aspect of the lower thorax. Spleen is felt at the deep inspiratory phase.

questions.question: Identify the papillae from the given histological section.
questions.explanation:
The given histological image is a section of the tongue showing circumvallate papillae, the largest papillae of the tongue.

Circumvallate papillae are large cylindrical structures that are around 8-12 in number, covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

They are arranged in a V-shaped row immediately in front of the sulcus terminalis (not on the sides of the tongue) on the dorsal surface of the tongue. It is narrower at its base than its apex. 

Numerous taste buds (around 250 taste buds for each of the 8-12 papillae) are present within the papillary walls and they contain chemosensory cells that synapse with the gustatory nerves. Serous glands of von Ebner empty via the ducts into the base of the sulcus.

Identification: They can be identified by their characteristic dome-shaped structure lined by stratified squamous epithelium.



Other options: 

Option A - Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red in color and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. It is supplied by the lingual nerve.

Option C- Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on the dorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. All except filiform papillae contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. It is supplied by the lingual nerve.

Option D - Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 7-year-old boy was brought to the hospital with multiple fractures of the humerus secondary to a fall from height. On examination, there is difficulty in flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm, and associated loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm. Which is the nerve most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette in a patient with difficulty in flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm, with associated loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm, is suggestive of injury to the musculocutaneous nerve.

Fall from a height on an outstretched hand is one of the main causes of humerus fractures.

Course:

The musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7) is a branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. It emerges at the lower border of the pectoralis minor and pierces coracobrachialis. It then descends between biceps brachii and brachialis where it supplies a branch to the shaft of the humerus. Then it enters the elbow and continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

It innervates all the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm i.e., 

  • Biceps brachii - involved in flexion of elbow and supination of the forearm
  • Brachialis -  involved in the flexion of the elbow
  • Coracobrachialis - flexes the arm at the glenohumeral joint

Cutaneous innervation of the lateral aspect of the forearm is by a branch of the musculocutaneous nerve, namely, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (C5, C6).

Hence, injury to the musculocutaneous nerve results in weakness of supination of forearm (biceps brachii), weakness in flexion of the elbow (biceps brachii, brachialis), and loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm (lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm).

Muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm:

Muscles Origin Insertion Innervation
Coracobrachialis Coracoid Process of scapula The medial side of the midshaft of the humerus Musculocutaneous nerve
Brachialis Distal half of anterior aspect of the humerus Ulnar tuberosity Musculocutaneous and radial nerve
Biceps Brachii Short head: Coracoid process 
Long head: Supraglenoid tubercle		 Radial tuberosity Musculocutaneous nerve

The below image shows the anterior compartment of the arm



Other options: 

Option A:

Median nerve injury is characterized by sensory loss over the radial 3 1/2 fingers and loss of thumb abduction. In high lesions, the long flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers, the radial wrist flexors, and the forearm pronator muscles are also paralyzed. Wasting of the thenar eminence is seen in long-standing cases.

Option B:

Radial nerve injury can present with wrist drop, thumb drop, and finger drop. Extension of the elbow will be spared in lesions below the elbow. The extension of the IP joints is intact due to the action of the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Loss of sensation over the first dorsal web space is observed.

Option D:

Ulnar nerve injury is characterized by ulnar claw hand, wasting of the hypothenar muscles and intrinsic muscles of the hand, and sensory loss over palmar & dorsal aspect of the medial third of the hand and medial 1 1/2 fingers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presented with jaw swelling and weight loss. Suspecting a malignancy, the submandibular gland was resected. Which is the most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection?
questions.explanation:
The most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection is the lingual nerve.

It loops around the submandibular duct and hence is susceptible to injury during submandibular gland resection.

Course:

The lingual nerve arises from the posterior trunk of the mandibular nerve (V3 branch of the trigeminal nerve). The lingual nerve descends between the tensor veli palatini muscle and the lateral pterygoid muscle, where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve. It then descends across the medial pterygoid muscle to enter the oral cavity. As the lingual nerve enters the floor of the oral cavity, it lies on the deep portion of the submandibular gland. It then passes into the tongue on the hyoglossus muscle where it is attached to the submandibular ganglion.

The submandibular duct lies between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves, superficial to the hyoglossus muscle. As the duct reaches the anterior border of the hyoglossus, it is crossed by the lingual nerve and lies in close proximity to the nerve. Hence lingual nerve injury is the most common.

Injury: 

The lingual nerve is at risk to be injured during submandibular gland resection because dissection of the submandibular duct from the nerve is required. Also, it is connected to the submandibular ganglion which will lead to the nerve being exposed within the operating field.

The manifestations of lingual nerve injury depend on whether the lesion is proximal or distal to where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve.

  • Proximal injury: There is loss of sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, gingivae, oral mucosa, lower lip, and chin.
  • Distal injury: In addition to features of proximal injury, secretion from the salivary glands below the oral fissure and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is also lost. 

Note:

The cranial nerves that are at risk during submandibular gland resection include:

  • The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
  • Lingual nerve
  • Hypoglossal nerve


Other options: 

Option A: Nerve to mylohyoid is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve and lies in the mylohyoid groove inferior to the mandibular foramen, hence the risk of injury is less.

Option B: Inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular canal via the mandibular foramen, hence is unlikely to be injured during submandibular gland excision.

Option D: Hypoglossal nerve injury is less common than lingual nerve injury as it only lies below and parallels to the submandibular duct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient underwent a coronary bypass graft with the great saphenous vein. The patient now complains of paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette in a patient with paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot is suggestive of injury to the saphenous nerve.

Injury to the saphenous nerve is common following venous cut down for access to the great saphenous vein, in this case for coronary bypass graft.

Saphenous nerve:

It is the longest and largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve and is the longest nerve in the body. It arises from the posterior division of the femoral nerve. It then enters the adductor canal and exits it by piercing the fascia lata between the gracilis and sartorius and supplies the skin over the patella. The saphenous nerve then descends along the medial border of the tibia along with the great saphenous vein (anterior to the vein) and supplies the skin on the medial side of the knee, leg, and foot as far as up to the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

Saphenous nerve injury:

When the great saphenous vein is being harvested for coronary bypass graft, injury to the saphenous nerve is common as it closely travels with the great saphenous vein. Sensory loss over the medial side of the knee, leg, and foot is observed in saphenous nerve injury. 



Other options: 

Option A: Superficial peroneal nerve injury causes sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the leg and the dorsum of the foot.

Option C: Femoral nerve gives rise to anterior cutaneous branches, the saphenous nerve, and motor supply to the quadriceps and sartorius. Anterior cutaneous branches supply the skin on the anterior thigh and knee. If the saphenous nerve was not an option in the question, the femoral nerve would have been the next best answer. 

Option D: Sural nerve injury causes sensory loss over the posterior and lateral aspects of the distal third of the leg and lateral side of the foot and fifth toe. It is often used as an autologous peripheral nerve graft as it is readily identified and easy to harvest.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: During the clinical examination of the nervous system, which of the following nerves can be tested by touching the highlighted structure?
questions.explanation:
The structure marked in the given sagittal section of the head and neck is the uvula. The sensory supply to the uvula is by the glossopharyngeal nerve and it is tested in this case.

Nerve supply by glossopharyngeal nerve:

  • Sensory fibers to the uvula, tympanic cavity, pharyngotympanic tube, tonsils, fauces, nasopharynx, and posterior third of the tongue.
  • Motor fibers to the stylopharyngeus muscle
  • Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland
  • Gustatory fibers for the postsulcal part of the tongue.

Pharyngeal plexus:

The nerve supply of the pharynx is mainly from the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. It is formed by the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion. The vagus nerve provides the motor supply and the glossopharyngeal nerve provides the sensory supply.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve:

  • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
  • All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve)

Note:

Previously cranial root of the spinal accessory nerve was thought to contribute to the motor functions of the pharyngeal plexus, but recent evidence suggests that it is not a major part of the motor drive to the pharyngeal plexus.

Innervation of the soft palate:

General sensation - It is mostly carried by the lesser palatine nerve which is a branch of maxillary nerve. The sensation from posterior part is carried by the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and from the plexus around the tonsil which is formed by the tonsillar branches of the glossopharyngeal and lesser palatine nerves. 

Taste sensation - There are taste buds in the oral surface of soft palate and sensation from them is carried by the lesser palatine nerve.

Secretomotor supply - It is by the lesser palatine nerve via postganglionic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion.

Motor supply - It is by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve except for tensor veli palatini which is supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The structure marked A in the image below gives rise to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
The structure marked A is ventral mesentery. The falciform ligament is a derivative of the ventral mesentery.



Mesenteries are double layers of the peritoneum that enclose an organ and connect it to the body wall. They provide pathways for vessels, nerves, and lymphatics to and from the abdominal viscera.

  • Ventral mesentery: Only the foregut has a ventral mesentery. It is attached to the terminal part of the esophagus, the stomach, and the upper part of the duodenum. The ventral mesentery is derived from the septum transversum. When the liver grows into the mesenchyme of the septum transversum, it divides the ventral mesentery into 2 parts:
    • Lesser omentum- extends from the lower portion of the esophagus, the stomach, and the upper portion of the duodenum to the liver
    • Ligaments of the liver- all ligaments of the liver (falciform ligament, right and left triangular ligaments, and coronary ligaments), except ligamentum teres
  • Dorsal mesentery: The foregut, midgut, and hindgut have a dorsal mesentery. This connects the organs to the posterior abdominal wall. It runs from the lower end of the esophagus to the cloacal region of the hindgut. It has the following special names in different regions:
    • Dorsal mesogastrium (or greater omentum)- stomach 
    • Dorsal mesoduodenum- duodenum
    • Mesentery proper- jejunum and ileum
    • Mesoappendix- appendix
    • Transverse mesocolon- transverse colon
    • Sigmoid mesocolon- sigmoid colon
    • Gastrosplenic ligament (stomach to the spleen), lienorenal ligament (spleen to the left kidney), and gastrophrenic ligament (stomach to diaphragm) are derived from the dorsal mesentery.

questions.question: A patient underwent surgery for the varicose vein. He now complains of sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario in a patient with sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot is suggestive of injury to the saphenous nerve. Injury to the saphenous nerve is common following varicose vein surgery.

The saphenous nerve is the longest and largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve and is the longest nerve in the body. It arises from the posterior division of the femoral nerve. It then enters the adductor canal and exits it by piercing the fascia lata between the gracilis and sartorius and supplies the skin over the patella. The saphenous nerve then descends along the medial border of the tibia along with the great saphenous vein (anterior to the vein) and supplies the skin on the medial side of the knee, leg, and foot up to the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

During stripping of veins in varicose surgery, injury to the saphenous nerve is common as it closely travels with the great saphenous vein. Sensory loss over the medial side of the knee, leg, and foot is observed in saphenous nerve injury. 



Other options: 

Option A: Sural nerve injury causes sensory loss over the posterior and lateral aspects of the distal third of the leg and lateral side of the foot and fifth toe. It is often used as an autologous peripheral nerve graft as it is readily identified and easy to harvest.

Option B: Superficial peroneal nerve injury causes sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the leg and the dorsum of the foot. It also causes weakness of foot eversion.

questions.question: Identify the cartilage given below:
questions.explanation:
The given image shows prominent collagen fibers arranged in bundles with intervening rows of chondrocytes. This is suggestive of white fibrocartilage.

Microscopy of fibrocartilage shows the following:

  • Chondrocytes- round in shape (in tendons they are flattened and elongated)
  • Ground tissue with collagen fibers- type I collagen fibers

questions.question: A patient presents with a unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, and excessive lacrimation. He also complains of hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth. On examination, pupillary reaction, light reflex, and accommodation reflex are normal. Which of the following marked nerves is involved in the above scenario?

The above patient presents with features suggesting an involvement of the trigeminal nerve. The structure marked 3 is the trigeminal nerve.

Other marked structures:

  • 1- Optic nerve. The normal visual field and light reflex rules out the involvement of the optic nerve.
  • 2- Oculomotor nerve. Normal accommodation and pupillary reflex rule out the involvement of the oculomotor nerve.
  • 4- Facial nerve. Absence of motor involvement of the face rule out the involvement of the facial nerve.


The trigeminal nerve leaves the anterior aspect of the pons as a small motor root and a large sensory root. The large sensory root expands to form the crescent-shaped trigeminal ganglion, which lies within a pouch of dura mater called the trigeminal or Meckel's cave. The ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerves arise from the anterior border of the ganglion.

Branches of the trigeminal nerve:

  • The ophthalmic nerve (V1)
    • Leaves the skull through the superior orbital fissure to enter the orbital cavity.
    • Contains only sensory fibers
      • Cornea (photophobia)
      • The skin of the forehead, scalp, eyelids, and nose
      • The mucous membrane of paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity
  • The maxillary nerve (V2)
    • Leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum.
    • Contains only sensory fibers from
      • Teeth of the upper jaw
      • The skin of the face over the maxilla
      • The mucous membrane of the nose, the maxillary sinus, and the palate
  • The mandibular nerve (V3)
    • Leaves the skull through the foramen ovale.
    • Contains both sensory and motor fibers.
    • Sensory from:
      • The skin of the cheek, over mandible, and side of the head
      • Teeth of the lower jaw and temporomandibular joint (hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth)
      • The mucous membrane of the mouth and anterior part of the tongue
    • Motor to:
      • Muscles of mastication (pterygoids, masseter, and temporalis)
      • Tensor tympani
      • Anterior belly of digastric
      • Mylohyoid

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the given structure:
questions.explanation:
The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas.



The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types:

  • Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells:
    • α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon 
    • β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin 
    • δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin
    • PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility. 
  • Minor cell types:
    • D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and hyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea.
    • Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause carcinoid syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists of an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primary follicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center.

The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullary sinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes.

The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node. 



Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes.

The glomerular tuft is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix.

The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus.



Option C: Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. It contains round white pulp surrounded by red pulp. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery or arterioles. Lymphocytes surrounding the arteriole are called peri-arterial lymphatic sheath (PALS) and contain T cells. Follicles in white pulp contain B cells.

The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It is like a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of sinusoids.

The image given below shows the histology of the spleen.

questions.question:
Which of the following muscles are supplied by Superior Gluteal Nerve?
  1. Gluteus Medius
  2. Gluteus Minimus
  3. Tensor fascia lata
  4. Piriformis
questions.explanation:
Gluteus Medius, Gluteus Minimus, and Tensor fascia lata are supplied by Superior Gluteal Nerve. Piriformis is supplied by the nerve to the piriformis. 

The dorsal branches of the L4, L5, and S1 rami give rise to the superior gluteal nerve. It is accompanied by superior gluteal vessels. This nerve leaves the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis and divides into superior and inferior branches. It supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae.

The dorsal divisions of the S1 and S2 rami give rise to the nerve to the piriformis. 

Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis on the femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject to stand on one limb. If the ipsilateral abductors are normal, the pelvis remains in a horizontal position. If the ipsilateral abductors are weak, then the pelvis tilts towards the opposite (unsupported) side. This is called positive Trendelenburg’s sign.

questions.question: A 25-year-old male presented with symptoms of inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits. He was also not able to hold a piece of paper between his fingers. What is the likely site of injury?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical situation with a positive card test and an inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits, suggests an ulnar nerve injury. The most likely site of injury would thus be medial epicondyle: site C

Injury at the medial epicondyle damages the ulnar nerve, leading to paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris (loss of ulnar deviation) and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (loss of distal interphalangeal joint flexion). It leads to hypothenar paralysis (lead to atrophy) and sensory loss. Also, flexor digitorum superficialis (supplied by median nerve) and extensor digitorum (supplied by the radial nerve) are still functional. Hence complete paralysis of the 3rd and 4th digits is not seen.  The positive card test is due to the weakness of palmar interossei leading to loss of adduction.

Ulnar nerve branches and supply: 

Superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis, skin on the palmar surface of medial 1½ fingers. The deep branch runs within the concavity of deep palmar arch and supplies all intrinsic muscles of the hand (except first 2 lumbricals and thenar muscles).

questions.question:
Which of the following muscles form the pelvic diaphragm?

A. Iliococcygeus
B. Pubococcygeus
C. Obturator internus
D. Deep transverse perinei
questions.explanation:
Iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus are parts of the pelvic diaphragm, which is also known as the levator ani.

The levator ani muscle is a complex unit that consists of 3 muscle components:

  • Pubococcygeus
    • Pubovaginalis - elevates the urethra and hence contributes to urinary continence
    • Puboperinealis - draws the perineal body towards the pubic symphysis
    • Puboanalis - elevates the anus and keeps the urogenital hiatus narrowed
  • Puborectalis
  • Iliococcygeus

Levator ani muscles are the most important muscles in the pelvic floor and maintain a constant state of contraction. They provide a stable floor and support the weight of the abdominopelvic contents against intra-abdominal forces. Weakening of levator ani and pelvic fascia from stretching or tearing during childbirth, may decrease support for the vagina, bladder, uterus, or rectum or alter the position of the neck of the bladder and urethra.

Other options: 

The obturator internus forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa and is not a part of the levator ani.

The deep transverse perineal muscle is the content of the deep perineal space and contributes to the formation of the perineal body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Given below is the image of a 33-hour chick embryo. Which of the following is derived from the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
The structure marked in the given image is the para-axial mesoderm. The ribs are derived from the para-axial mesoderm.

During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, which refers to the formation of the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. This is followed by the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, which induces the formation of the neural tube above it. During the formation of the neural tube, some cells at the lateral border dissociate and form the neural crest cells, which is sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer.



After the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, the mesoderm on either side can be seen to be organized into three layers as follows:

1. Para-axial mesoderm - Thickened plate of the mesoderm close to the midline, on either side of the notochord. This forms the somitomeres and somites, which have the following derivatives: 

  • Dermatome: Forms the segmental dermis of the skin
  • Myotome: Forms the skeletal muscle
  • Sclerotome: Forms the vertebral column and ribs

2. Intermediate mesoderm - Longitudinal strip of mesoderm that connects the para-axial with the lateral plate mesoderm. The urinary (Option A) and genital systems are derived from the intermediate mesoderm.

3. Lateral plate mesoderm - A thinner layer of mesoderm that lies laterally. This layer develops a large cavity called the intraembryonic coelom that gives rise to pericardial, pleural (Option C), and peritoneal cavities.

The neural crest cells also contribute to the formation of structures as follows:

In the trunk region, they form melanocytes, sensory ganglia (Option B), sympathetic and enteric neurons, Schwann cells, and adrenal medulla cells.
In the cranial region, they contribute to the craniofacial skeleton, neurons for cranial ganglia, satellite glial cells, and melanocytes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the structure marked as A.
questions.explanation:
The arrow-marked structure in the given image is the terminal bronchiole. It can be identified by the absence of cartilage, which would be present in the bronchus, and the presence of cilia and stratified columnar epithelium, which would not be seen in respiratory bronchioles and alveolar sac.

The following is a summary of the intrapulmonary passages:

Trachea → Main Bronchi → Lobar Bronchi → Segmental Bronchi → Terminal Bronchiole → Respiratory Bronchiole → Alveolar Duct → Alveolar Sac → Alveoli

Bronchi and bronchioles can be distinguished by the presence of cartilage and glands in the bronchi which are not present in the bronchioles.

Terminal bronchioles represent the most distal parts of the conducting passage. Each terminal bronchiole ends by dividing into respiratory bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles contain cilia and stratified columnar epithelium, whereas respiratory bronchioles contain few or no cilia, and simple cuboidal epithelium. Another differentiating point between the two is that terminal bronchioles would not communicate with the alveoli but respiratory bronchioles would have a communication with the alveoli.

Each respiratory bronchiole ends by dividing into a few alveolar ducts. Each alveolar duct ends in a passage, the atrium, which leads into a number of rounded alveolar sacs. Each alveolar sac is studded with a number of air sacs or alveoli.

questions.question: A patient's right hip drops when he takes the right foot off the ground. Which of the following would not be involved in the patient?

A patient with dropping of the right hip on lifting the right foot off the ground, has a positive Trendelenburg’s sign. The sciatic nerve would not be involved.

A positive Trendelenburg's sign is seen in the paralysis of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles, both of which are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. In the scenario mentioned, since the patient has dropping of the hip on the right side, the structures on the left side would be affected.



Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus: 

  • When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground,  making it the unsupported side,  gluteus medius and minimus muscles on the opposite side, which is the supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.
  • When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis on the unsupported side sinks when the patient lifts the foot off the ground. This causes the patients to have a characteristic lurching gait.

questions.explanation:
The image shows a sacrococcygeal teratoma, which occurs due to the persistence of pluripotent cells of the primitive streak in the sacrococcygeal region.

During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, which refers to the formation of the three germ layers. These germ layers are formed from the primordial germ cells of the epiblast, which are pluripotent. The process begins with the formation of the primitive streak on the epiblast, which develops into the primitive node in the cranial region, and a primitive pit. The cells from the epiblast, migrate towards the primitive streak and invaginate into the primitive pit and organizes itself into cells arranged in three layers, which eventually develop into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The prechordal plate simply refers to the cells that have invaginated in the cranial region.



Sacrococcygeal teratomas occur due to remnants of pluripotent cells from the primitive streak due to defective migration of the cells (Option B). As these cells are from the epiblast, teratomas contain tissues from all germ layers which may include skin, hair, cartilage and bone (Option C). These tumors are benign in nature (Option D), but may rarely become malignant. If they occur in the cranial end of the primitive streak, they form oro-pharyngeal teratomas (as shown below), whereas if they occur in the caudal end of the primitive streak in the coccygeal region, they are called sacro-coccygeal teratomas.

The basal ganglia refers to the mass of grey matter located within the cerebral white matter and is responsible for a number of coordinated functions including the control of extra-pyramidal pathways for motor coordination. questions.question: On neurologic examination, a patient is not able to identify an object but is able to recognize the object from its texture, colour and pattern. Which of the following is likely to have been affected?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario suggests that the patient has visual agnosia and the likely site of involvement would be the inferior temporal lobe.

  • Agnosia refers to the inability to visually identify objects and is also called optic aphasia. According to De Jong, visual agnosia is further classified into:
    • Apperceptive visual agnosia - the visual image appears distorted to the patient and hence they are unable to recognise it. This occurs due lesions in the parieto-occipital region
    • Associative visual agnosia - inability to visually identify objects in the absence of visual impairment, with ability to identify the object using other sensory modalities (as suggested in the scenario). This occurs due to lesions of occipito-temporal junction, which is present in the inferior temporal lobe. Prosopagnosia is a type of associatetive visual agnosia which refers to the inability to visually identify faces. 

The occipital lobe acts as the primary visual area and a lesion in this region would result in cortical blindness and achromatopsia, which is the inability to visualise colour. In the given scenario, as the patient is also able to identify colour, it indicates that the occipital lobe (Option A) is unaffected and (hence inferior temporal lobe is the better answer). 

Stereognosis is the ability to identify an object by a perception of the form and nature of an object without looking at it. In the given scenario, the patient is able to recognize the object from its texture and pattern which indicates that stereognosis is intact. Loss of this ability is known as astereognosis which occurs in lesions of the superior parietal lobule (Options B and C) and dorsal column pathways.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Apocrine glands are present in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Apocrine glands are present in the axilla.

Exocrine glands can be classified into three subtypes, based on the manner in which their secretions are poured out of the cells:

  1. Apocrine 
  2. Merocrine
  3. Holocrine

In apocrine glands, the apical parts of the cells are shed off to discharge the secretion. Examples of apocrine glands are :

  • Secretion of milk fat by mammary glands
  • Atypical sweat glands in the axilla, perianal region, periumbilical skin, mons pubis.
  • Ceruminous glands of the external auditory meatus are modified apocrine glands

Apocrine glands are large glands found in the dermis or subcutaneous fat. They are a type of sweat gland. It consists of a basal secretory coil followed by a straight duct that opens into the pilary canal above the duct of the sebaceous gland. In hairless skin, it directly opens onto the skin surface. 

Apocrine activity is minimal before puberty, after which it is androgen-dependent and responsive to emotional stimuli. It is controlled by adrenergic nerves and is sensitive to adrenaline and noradrenaline. The secretion is initially sterile and odorless, but it undergoes bacterial decomposition to generate odorous and musky compounds. Obstruction of apocrine sweat ducts and associated upper hair follicles in the axillae, breast areolae, and pubic region, mainly in women, is thought to cause Fox–Fordyce disease. It is also implicated in the causation of a painful, occasionally debilitating condition called hidradenitis suppurativa.

questions.question: 2. A patient presents with carcinoma near the anal opening. Which among the following lymph nodes are most likely to be involved first?
questions.explanation:
In a patient with carcinoma near the anal opening, superficial inguinal lymph nodes are most likely to be involved first. The tumor in the given clinical scenario is located near the anal opening, which means that it lies below the pectinate line. Lesions below this line typically drain lymph to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, making them the most likely site for metastasis. The anal canal measures approximately 3.8 cm in length and extends from the anorectal junction to the anus. It is divided into three parts: * The upper mucosal part is 15 mm long, is endodermal in origin, and contains the anal columns and anal sinuses. The pectinate line marks the junction between the upper mucosal part and the middle transitional zone. * The middle transitional zone is 15 mm long, is also lined by mucous membrane, and is ectodermal in origin. The lower boundary of this part often appears whitish and is referred to as the white line of Hilton. * The lowest cutaneous part is 8 mm long, is lined by keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium, and contains sebaceous glands. Lymphatic drainage from the region above the pectinate line is directed to the internal iliac lymph nodes (option B), whereas drainage from the region below this line is directed to the medial group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes. The pectinate line serves as the watershed line of the anal canal.

The image above shows a patent ductus arteriosus due to a defect in the left side of the 6th aortic arch. Usually, in term infants, the ductus arteriosus closes within 72 hours of birth. Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). PDA usually presents with a hyperdynamic precordium, bounding peripheral pulses, wide pulse pressure, a machine-like continuous or systolic murmur, cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, hepatomegaly, increasing oxygen dependence, carbon dioxide retention, and renal failure. In a majority of cases, PDA closes spontaneously. If spontaneous closure fails to occur, COX inhibitors like indomethacin or ibuprofen can be used. Surgical ligation is indicated in case of contraindications to medical management or failure of the same. Defects involving the 4th left aortic arch could cause a variety of aortic arch anomalies, such as interruption of the aortic arch, but not PDA. Option C: The 6th right aortic arch forms the proximal part of the right pulmonary artery. questions.question: 7. A patient presents with pain on the lateral side of the thigh. The doctor diagnosed him with meralgia paresthetica. Identify the nerve affected?
questions.explanation:
Meralgia paresthetica is a neuropathic pain syndrome affecting the anterolateral thigh due to compression or entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN), which is marked as "3" in the given image. The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises from the posterior divisions of the ventral rami of L2 and L3, and it supplies the skin of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the thigh up to the knee. It is prone to injury, especially as it leaves the pelvis deep to the inguinal ligament, just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. The angulation of the nerve as it crosses the iliac crest makes it vulnerable to compression during hip extension, which may increase angulation and tension on the nerve. Patients may develop meralgia paresthetica as a complication of inguinal hernia repair. The initial management of this nerve entrapment involves conservative measures like rest, application of ice, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), physical therapy, and local injections of corticosteroids and anesthetics.
