questions.question: The spinal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve has 2nd order neurons to carry which sensation?
questions.explanation:
The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions. The first-order neurons for each division originate from different sensory ganglia:

1.Ophthalmic Division (V1):
   First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion (also called the semilunar or Gasserian ganglion).

2. Maxillary Division (V2):
   First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

3. Mandibular Division (V3):
   First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

These first-order neurons carry sensory information from the face to the brainstem. Upon entering the brainstem, the fibers synapse with second-order neurons in specific nuclei:

1. Principal Sensory Nucleus (Main Sensory Nucleus):
    a.Receives input from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve.
    b.Located in the pons.
    c.Second-order neurons here carry discriminative touch and proprioceptive information.

2. Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus (Spinal Nucleus of Trigeminal):
   a.Receives input mainly from the maxillary and mandibular divisions.
   b.Located in the medulla.
   c.Second-order neurons here carry pain and temperature sensations.

After synapsing in these nuclei, the sensory information is further relayed to higher brain centers for processing and perception.

The tail of the caudate nucleus is not seen on the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. It is present on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

The inferior horn is the largest compartment of the lateral ventricle and extends up to 2.5 cm from the temporal pole. The relations are: 

Roof - Tapetum of corpus callosum laterally and tail of caudate nucleus medially.

Floor (lateral to medial) - Collateral eminence produced by collateral fissure, hippocampus.

The floor of the temporal horn consists of the hippocampus medially and the collateral eminence, formed by the infolding of the collateral sulcus, laterally. The inferior part of the choroidal fissure, located between the fimbria of the fornix and the inferolateral aspect of the thalamus, lies in the medial wall. 

The lateral ventricle is divided into the body and 3 horns. The locations of the parts are: 

  • Body - parietal lobe
  • Anterior horn - frontal lobe
  • Posterior horn - occipital lobe
  • Inferior horn - temporal lobe.


The anterior horn extends from the genu of the corpus callosum up to the interventricular foramen. The relations of the anterior horn are: 

  • Anteriorly - Genu and rostrum of the corpus callosum
  • Roof - Anterior part of the body of the corpus callosum
  • Floor and lateral wall - Caudate nucleus
  • Medial wall - Septum pellucidum and anterior column of fornix

The body or central part extends from the interventricular foramen to the splenium of the corpus callosum. The relations of the body are: 

  • Roof - Body of the corpus callosum
  • Medial wall - Septum pellucidum
  • Floor (from lateral to medial) - Caudate nucleus, stria terminalis, thalamostriate vein, thalamus, choroid plexus, and body of the fornix

The posterior horn extends from the splenium to the occipital pole. The relations are: 

  • Roof and lateral wall - Tapetum of corpus callosum
  • Medial wall - Forceps major and calcar avis (calcarine sulcus

Note: There is no lateral wall for the lateral ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following marked areas in the histopathological specimen shows calcification?
questions.explanation:
The given specimen is that of an epiphyseal cartilage, where zone 3 corresponds to the zone of calcification.

Epiphyseal cartilage is divided into five zones :

  • The resting zone consists of hyaline cartilage without morphological changes in the cells (option 1)
  • In the proliferative zone, chondrocytes divide rapidly and form columns of stacked cells parallel to the long axis of the bone (option 2)
  • The hypertrophic cartilage zone contains large chondrocytes whose cytoplasm has accumulated glycogen. The resorbed matrix is reduced to thin septa between the chondrocytes.
  • Simultaneous with the death of chondrocytes in the calcified cartilage zone, the thin septa of cartilage matrix become calcified by the deposit of hydroxyapatite.
  • In the ossification zone, endochondral bone tissue appears (option 4). Blood capillaries and osteoprogenitor cells formed by mitosis of cells originating from the periosteum invade the cavities left by the chondrocytes. The osteoprogenitor cells form osteoblasts, which are distributed in a discontinuous layer over the septa of the calcified cartilage matrix. Ultimately, the osteoblasts deposit bone matrix over the three-dimensional calcified cartilage matrix.

The epiphyseal cartilage is responsible for the growth in the length of bone and it disappears in adults, which is why bone growth ceases in adulthood.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true concerning the anatomy of the breast?
options: Inner quadrants contain most breast tissue
Ligaments of cooper are found only in lower quadrants
Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold
questions.correct_answer: Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold
questions.explanation:
The tail of Spence extends across the anterior axillary fold and is a small extension of the upper lateral quadrant of the breast.

The breast lies in the superficial fascia of the pectoral region. It is divided into four quadrants, i.e. upper medial, upper lateral, lower medial and lower lateral. 

Vertically, it extends from the second to the sixth ribs. Horizontally, it extends from the lateral border of the sternum to the midaxillary line. A small extension of the upper lateral quadrant, called the axillary tail of Spence, passes through an opening in the deep fascia and lies in the axilla. The opening is called the foramen of Langer. 

The breast lies on the deep pectoral fascia covering the pectoralis major and serratus anterior superiorly, the external abdominal oblique and its aponeurosis inferiorly, and the clavipectoral fascia laterally. Fibrous strands or sheets consisting of condensations of connective tissue extend between the posterior lamina of the superficial fascia and the dermis. These suspensory ligaments (retinacula or Cooper’s ligaments) are often well-developed in the superior parts of the breast and support the breast tissue, helping to minimize drooping.

The breasts normally comprise up to 20 discrete lobes that contain ductal-glandular tissue consisting of branching ducts and terminal secretory lobules in a connective tissue stroma. Each lobe is derived by branching from one central lactiferous duct in the nipple. The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU or lobule) is the functional milk secretory component of the breast. 

The upper outer quadrant of the breast contains a greater volume of tissue than the other quadrants. This is the reason for the majority of the carcinomas arising in the upper outer quadrant.

The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion. It is a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), the most prominent sulcus of the cerebral hemisphere. It separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. Deep to the lateral sulcus lies the insular cortex.

  • The insular cortex and parts of the basal ganglia, such as the putamen, are located deep to the pterion, beneath the lateral sulcus.
  • Stem of the lateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian fissure. It houses the middle cerebral artery and its branches, playing a crucial role in brain vascularization and cortical organization.

During surgeries, the pterion is a common site for trephining (making a hole in the skull).

The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression. It is innervated by the facial nerve. It is known as the whistling muscle.

The buccinator muscle is primarily responsible for keeping food between the teeth during mastication by pressing the cheek against the teeth (involved in flattening the cheeks against the gums and teeth).

In facial nerve palsy, paralysis of the buccinator muscle can lead to food accumulating in the cheek pouch, as the muscle is unable to contract properly.

Other options:

Option B: Levator Labii Superioris: This muscle elevates the upper lip and contributes to facial expressions like showing the upper teeth and dilates the nostrils. It is not involved in keeping food in place during chewing.

Option C : Zygomaticus Major: Responsible for pulling the corner of the mouth upward and outward, contributing to smiling. It does not influence food placement during mastication.

Option D : Orbicularis Oris: Encircles the mouth and helps in closing the lips. While it is involved in mastication and speech, its paralysis would not cause food to accumulate in the cheek.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is not a derivative of neural crest cells?
questions.explanation:
Retinal pigment epithelium is not a derivative of neural crest cells.

Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm. The RPE develops from the outer layer of the optic cup, a structure that arises from the neural tube (neuroectodermal origin), not from neural crest cells.

Neural crest cells are a group of cells that migrate during embryonic development and give rise to various structures, including parts of the nervous system, face, and heart.

Neural crest cells (NCC) are present adjacent to the neural tube and are sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer. It contributes to the formation of many organs and tissues:

In the trunk region, they form: 

  • Melanocytes (Option D)
  • Sensory ganglia
  • Sympathetic and enteric neurons
  • Schwann cells 
  • Adrenal medulla cells

In the cranial region, they contribute to the: 

  • Craniofacial skeleton
  • Neurons for cranial ganglia-Ciliary ganglion  (Option C)
  • Ciliary muscles  (Option A)
  • Satellite glial cells
  • Melanocytes

Some of the other neural crest derivatives are:

  • C cells of the thyroid gland
  • Conotruncal septum in the heart
  • Odontoblasts
  • Smooth muscle cells to blood vessels to the face and forebrain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The cranial component of the neural crest cells leads to the formation of?
questions.explanation:
The cranial component of neural crest cells (NCC) leads to the formation of Conotruncal septum.

The conotruncal septum is also known as the aortopulmonary septum. The formation of the aortopulmonary septum in the truncus arteriosus divides the outflow channel of the heart into the ventral aorta and the pulmonary trunk. Persistent truncus arteriosus results when the conotruncal ridges fail to form. 

The development of the heart begins in the third week of embryogenesis with the formation of the cardiogenic mesoderm. The heart tube forms through fusion of paired endocardial tubes, which then undergo looping and septation to establish the four chambers. By the end of the eighth week, the heart achieves its definitive structure, with separate atria, ventricles, and major vessels.

The heart develops from mesodermal origins, with different parts deriving from specific embryonic structures:

  • First Heart Field (Primary Heart Field): Forms the left ventricle and part of the atria.
  • Second Heart Field: Contributes to the right ventricle, outflow tract (conus arteriosus and truncus arteriosus), and part of the atria.
  • Neural Crest Cells: Contribute to the septation of the outflow tract and the formation of the aorticopulmonary septum.
  • Proepicardium (Epicardial Cells): Forms the epicardium and contributes to coronary vessels.
  • Sinus Venosus: Forms part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) and the coronary sinus.
  • Endocardial Cushions: Form the atrioventricular valves and contribute to septation.

Other options:

Option A: SA node is derived from the primary heart field - sinus venosus.

Option B: AV cushions are derived from adjacent endocardial cells. The endocardial cells along with the epicardium and mesenchyme, form the AV cushions.

Option D: Chordae tendineae are formed from mesenchymal tissue within the heart.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy underwent splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenic purpura. During the procedure, the surgeon noticed bleeding while separating the spleen from the stomach. Which vessels are most likely implicated in this bleeding?

This patient, undergoing splenectomy, while separating the spleen from the stomach, is likely bleeding from the short gastric vessels.

In an open splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament is opened and short gastric vessels are ligated and divided.

The spleen is attached to the stomach through the gastrosplenic ligament. The gastrosplenic ligament attaches the greater curvature of stomach to the upper pole of the spleen.



Contents of the gastrosplenic ligament include:

  • Short gastric vessels
  • Left gastroepiploic vessels

Hence, while separating the spleen from the stomach, there are maximum chances of bleeding if there is injury to the short gastric vessels.

Other Options:

Option A: Left gastric vessels: Left gastric vessels run along the lesser curvature of the stomach. It is unlikely to be the source of bleeding in this case.

Option C: Right gastro-epiploic vessels: The right gastroepiploic vessels run along the pylorus and inferior region of the greater curvature of the stomach. It is not a part of the gastrosplenic ligament.

Option D: Splenic vessels: The splenic artery and vein run along the superior border of the pancreas. They are not directly involved in the separation of the spleen from the stomach.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the marked structure
questions.explanation:
The marked structure is the primitive streak.

The primitive streak appears in the early stages of gastrulation, a process that reorganizes the epiblast into three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. It appears as a linear thickening on the dorsal surface of the epiblast in the bilaminar embryonic disc. It is found in the caudal (tail-end) region of the developing embryo.



Functions of the primitive streak:

  • Serves as the site where cells migrate inward to form the mesoderm and endoderm.
  • Marks the beginning of gastrulation.
  • Defines the body axis (head-to-tail, left-to-right).

Other Options:

Option B: Notochord: A rod-like structure derived from mesoderm that forms after the primitive streak and is crucial for the development of the neural tube. Located cranially relative to the primitive streak.



Option C: Neural Groove: A depression in the ectoderm that forms during neurulation, leading to the development of the neural tube. It appears after the primitive streak.

Option D: Secondary Neural Plate: Part of the neural plate involved in the later stages of neural tube development. It is not directly related to the primitive streak.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak?
questions.explanation:
Endoderm is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak.

Gastrulation is when the single-layered blastula reorganizes into a multi-layered structure called the gastrula. This process establishes the three primary germ layers that give rise to all tissues and organs of the body. During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form the three germ layers: endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm.

Cells from the epiblast migrate inward (invagination) through the primitive streak.

The first group of migrating epiblast cells replaces the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm. The endoderm gives rise to structures like the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and lungs. 

Subsequent migrating cells spread between the epiblast and the newly formed endoderm to create the mesoderm, which forms structures like muscles, bones, and the cardiovascular system.

Remaining epiblast cells that do not migrate through the primitive streak form the ectoderm, which gives rise to the epidermis and the nervous system.



Other Options:

Option B: Cardiac Mesoderm: The mesoderm forms after the endoderm and differentiates later into subtypes, including the cardiac mesoderm.

Option C: Epidermis: The epidermis arises from the ectoderm, which forms after both the endoderm and mesoderm.

Option D: Neural Groove: The neural groove is part of the ectoderm and forms during neurulation, which occurs much later than the formation of the endoderm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: During walking, the hip bone on the side of the suspended leg is raised by the action of which muscle present in the supporting leg?
questions.explanation:
Gluteus Medius of the supporting leg is responsible for raising the hip bone on the side of the suspended leg.

Actions of Gluteus Medius:

  •  Hip abduction
  •  Stabilizes the pelvis during gait.
  •  Assists the internal rotation of the thigh.

Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis on the femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject to stand on one limb.

Trendelenburg Sign:
Trendelenburg sign is a clinical sign used to assess the function of the gluteus medius.
It is positive when the pelvis drops on the opposite side of the stance leg, indicating weakness or dysfunction of the gluteus medius on the supporting leg.
In a healthy individual, the gluteus medius contracts to prevent the pelvis from tilting when one leg is lifted. If the gluteus medius is weak or paralyzed, the pelvis tilts toward the side of the suspended leg.



Option B: Gluteus Maximus: Extends and externally rotates the hip; key for climbing stairs and rising from sitting. Weakness causes difficulty in hip extension, affecting activities like standing up or climbing.

Option C: Obturator Internus: Externally rotates and stabilizes the hip joint; abducts the thigh when the hip is flexed. Dysfunction can impair hip rotation, commonly affected in pelvic injuries.

Option D: Quadratus Femoris: Externally rotates and adducts the hip. Injury or entrapment of the nerve to quadratus femoris can cause deep hip pain and weakness in rotation.

questions.question: Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve leads to?
options: Loss of extension of the wrist
questions.explanation:
Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve leads to loss of extension of digits.

The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is a continuation of the deep branch of the radial nerve. It originates from the radial nerve in the cubital fossa, near the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. After passing through the supinator muscle, it transitions into the PIN.

The PIN is purely a motor nerve and supplies the posterior compartment of the forearm.

Thumb drop, finger drop

Monteggia fracture involves a fracture of the proximal ulna with a dislocation of the radial head. The radial nerve, especially its posterior interosseous branch, is at risk due to its proximity to the fracture site and leads to loss of extension of digits.

questions.explanation:
The muscle marked in the above image is the lateral pterygoid muscle and its primary function is depression of the mandible (opening of the mouth). 

Bilateral contraction of the lateral pterygoid alone causes depression of the mandible (making it the primary function) whereas, protrusion is the result of bilateral contraction of both the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles. 

The lateral pterygoid has the following actions:

  1. Opening of the jaw (depression): Lateral pterygoid has a specialized role in mandibular opening mediated by its horizontal fibres. When left and right lateral pterygoid muscles contract together, the mandibular condyle is pulled forwards and slightly downwards.   2. Side-to-side movement: When the lateral pterygoid contracts unilaterally along with the adjacent medial pterygoid the jaw is pulled medially. This is used for grinding food between teeth of the same side. This action is mediated by the inferior head of the lateral pterygoid.

questions.question: What represents the marked area in the given histology of lymph node?
questions.explanation:
The area marked in the image is the mantle zone of a lymph node.

Lymph node has primary follicle composed of small, quiescent lymphocytes, and a secondary follicle with germinal centre composed mainly of antigen-stimulated B cells.

The mantle zone is produced as surrounding cells are marginalised by the rapidly growing germinal centre. It is populated by mainly quiescent B cells with condensed heterochromatic nuclei and little cytoplasm (hence the deeply basophilic staining of this region in routine preparations), a few helper T cells, Follicular Dendritic cells and macrophages.

In peripheral lymph nodes, the marginal zone are often inapparent because they are mixed with the mantle zone cells. And often not well developed in lymph nodes.

The paracortex lies between the cortical follicles and the medulla and is populated mainly by T cells, which are not organised into follicles

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A young patient presented with hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus and tetany. Which of the following marked areas in the picture is defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus, and tetany is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. It is caused by defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch. In the image of pharyngeal pouches, "3" points to the thymus (derivative of 3rd pharyngeal pouch). Since in the above question, the thymus is absent, option 3 will be the most appropriate answer.



DiGeorge syndrome is a complex embryopathy that is caused by the hemizygous interstitial deletion of chromosome 22. It is characterized by multiple developmental defects, including conotruncal defects, hypoparathyroidism, and dysmorphic syndrome. It is also known as velocardiofacial syndrome (palate, facial, and cardiac defects).

It has variable presentations including Cleft palate, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency, Cardiac defects, and Hypocalcemia secondary to parathyroid aplasia (CATCH-22).

questions.question: The joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib to the 7th rib is a:
questions.explanation:
The interchondral joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib with the 7th rib is a synovial joint.

Joints in the thoracic cavity are of the following types:

  • Synarthrosis - structures are connected by a fibrous band of tissue. E.g, 1st sternocostal joint
  • Synchondrosis - primary cartilaginous joints. E.g., costochondral joints
  • Symphysis - secondary cartilaginous joints. E.g. manubriosternal and xiphisternal joints 
  • Synovial joints - the presence of these help the thoracic cavity expand during inspiration. E.g.:
    • Interchondral joint
    • Sternocostal joint
    • Costovertebral joint
    • Costotransverse joint

Note: 

The interchondral joint between the 9th and 10th cartilages is never synovial and sometimes absent.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Foot drop is caused by damage to:
questions.explanation:
Foot drop is caused by damage to the common peroneal nerve.

The common peroneal nerve is a component of the sciatic nerve. In the posterior thigh, it supplies the short head of the biceps femoris. It curves around the neck of the fibula deep to peroneus longus and divides into superficial and deep peroneal nerves.

  • The superficial peroneal nerve innervates peroneus longus and peroneus brevis which are the evertors of the foot and to the skin over the dorsal area of the foot except for the first webspace and lateral side of the little toe.
  • The deep peroneal nerve innervates all muscles of the anterior compartment which are the dorsiflexors of the foot, extensor digitorum brevis, first two dorsal interossei muscles, and skin between great and second toes.

Hence, injury to the common peroneal nerve will lead to:

  • Weakness of dorsiflexion of foot or foot drop
  • Loss of eversion
  • Loss of extension of toes
  • Sensory loss
    • Anterior and lateral side of the leg
    • Dorsum of the foot including the medial side of the great toe

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: An absent gag reflex can result from injury to which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation:
An absent gag reflex can result from injury to the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) and the vagus nerve (X).

The afferent nerve for the gag reflex is the glossopharyngeal nerve, while the efferent nerve consists of both the glossopharyngeal (to the stylopharyngeus muscle) and vagus. Both these nerves pass through the jugular foramen and damage to them may be the cause for loss of gag reflex.

Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are:

  • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
  • All the muscles of the pharynx(except the stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve).

The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of the posterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate, etc. Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc.

The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing, phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx. 

Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include:

  • Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
  • By assessing the strength of the cough

questions.question: If a tumor compresses the structures passing through the opening marked in the given image, which of the following sensations would be affected?
options: Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose
questions.correct_answer: Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose
questions.explanation:
The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure. If a tumour compresses the structures passing through this foramen, it would impair sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose, as this would affect the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve.

The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face.

The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity. Therefore, if a tumour or lesion compresses the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure, it would likely affect the sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose because these areas are innervated by the branches of the trigeminal nerve that pass through this fissure.

Other options: 

Option A: Sensation of the nasopharynx is innervated by other branches of the trigeminal and glossopharyngeal nerve, not by structures passing through the superior orbital fissure.

Option B: While some sensation from the nasal cavity comes from the trigeminal nerve, the specific branches affected by a lesion in the superior orbital fissure are more focused on the anterior areas of the face.

Option D: Sensation of the chin is primarily innervated by the mandibular branch (CN V3) of the trigeminal nerve, which passes through the foramen ovale, not the superior orbital fissure.

questions.question: A chronic tobacco consumer went to the dental clinic with bleeding lesions on his tongue and was diagnosed with carcinoma of the tongue. Which of the following papillae, which do not have taste buds, is least likely to be involved in such a cancer?

Among the different types of papillae on the tongue, the one that does not have taste buds is the filiform papillae.

Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on the dorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. The filiform papillae do not contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

Other papillae of the tongue are: 

Circumvallate papillae are 8-12 in number which are large cylindrical structures. They form a V-shaped row just in front of the sulcus terminalis. Usually, the entire papillae are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. They are supplied by the facial nerve.

Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.question: Which artery is used for arteriovenous shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis, and is located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus?
questions.explanation:
The posterior tibial artery, located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, that is used for arteriovenous (AV) shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis.

The posterior tibial artery is situated behind the medial malleolus and approximately 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, making it a suitable site for creating an AV fistula with the great saphenous vein. This location allows for optimal access and ensures that the shunt can handle the necessary blood flow for effective dialysis with the great saphenous vein. However, they are not commonly used for AV shunting in common practices.

Arteries used for AV shunting include the radial artery and the brachial artery in the upper arm, which are frequently employed for hemodialysis access. In the lower leg, the anterior tibial artery and the peroneal (fibular) artery are less commonly used for this procedure. 

Other options:

Option D: The fibular circumflex artery is a small artery and is not commonly used for hemodialysis access. It is not a standard choice and does not fit the anatomical location described, as it is a branch of the anterior tibial artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the outer covering of the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion.

Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrude through the umbilicus. In this condition, the herniated organs are covered by both peritoneum and an amnion. The umbilical cord inserts directly into this sac, which helps in identifying the condition. The defect occurs due to the failure of the physiological hernia to return to the body cavity by the 11th week of gestation.

The size of an omphalocele can vary significantly. It may be relatively small, containing only the gut, or it can be classified as a giant omphalocele if it measures 4 cm or more in diameter, encompassing the gut, liver, and other abdominal organs. The condition is often associated with other congenital anomalies such as trisomies 13, 15, 18, or 21, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, and pentalogy of Cantrell.

Treatment for omphalocele involves covering the exposed organs to prevent fluid loss and protect them from infection. Prophylactic antibiotics may be administered in case of rupture. Surgical correction is usually performed once the baby is stable. In omphalocele, since the umbilicus is covered by a reflection of the amnion, this membrane also covers the omphalocele itself, differentiating it from other types of abdominal wall defects.



Note : Gastroschisis is a condition where the intestinal loops herniate through the defect in the abdominal wall. The defect usually lies on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly). The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion. It is associated with elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels.

questions.question: A patient presents with sciatica and tenderness in the hamstring muscles. Which nerve supplies the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The adductor magnus is the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition.

In sciatica, the sciatic nerve is typically affected, which branches into the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve. The adductor magnus muscle is an example of a hybrid muscle with dual innervation:

  • The adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve.
  • The hamstring part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the tibial nerve.

During sciatica, the tibial nerve is often affected, which would impact the hamstring part of the adductor magnus. However, because the adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve, it remains functional and is likely to be spared.

The obturator nerve arises from the anterior division of the ventral rami of L2-L4. Near the obturator foramen, it divides into anterior and posterior branches.

  • Anterior division supplies pectineus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, and gracilis
  • Posterior division supplies adductor magnus, obturator externus. It also supplies adductor brevis if the muscle is not supplied by the anterior division

The image given below shows the course of the obturator nerve.




Other options:

Option A: The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and can also be affected in sciatica. It is responsible for innervating muscles in the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg.

Option B: The tibial nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and is often affected in sciatica. It supplies the hamstring part of the adductor magnus, which would be impacted during sciatica.

Option C: The femoral nerve is not involved in sciatica. It supplies the quadriceps and other muscles in the anterior compartment of the thigh, and does not innervate the adductor magnus.

questions.question: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness during daily activities. On examination, she is unable to make an 'O' shape by opposing her thumb and index finger. Which of the following muscles is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
The difficulty in buttoning the shirt and the inability to make the "O" shape with fingers suggest the involvement of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.

This is a case of anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome. The AIN is a purely motor branch of the median nerve that affects specific muscles in the forearm, the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus leading to difficulty in performing tasks requiring fine motor control, such as the "OK" sign. Among the options provided, the abductor pollicis brevis is uniquely and consistently innervated by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve, making it susceptible to dysfunction in conditions affecting the median nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The opponens pollicis is innervated primarily by the lateral terminal branch of the median nerve, with some contributions from a branch of the deep terminal branch of the ulnar nerve. While it plays a role in thumb opposition, it is not consistently affected in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome, which primarily impacts deeper flexor muscles like the flexor pollicis longus. Therefore, it is less likely to be the cause of the patient’s inability to perform the "OK" sign.

Option B: The palmar interossei muscles are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Because they do not receive any innervation from the median nerve, they are not implicated in AIN syndrome. Their primary function involves the adduction of the fingers.

Option C: The flexor pollicis brevis has dual innervation: the superficial head is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, while the deep head is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. This dual supply makes it less likely to be solely affected in AIN syndrome.

However, the posterior cranial fossa also gets sensory supply from the C2, C3 fibres distributed by hypoglossal nerve and C2 fibres distributed by vagus nerve. questions.question: 4. The area marked by the arrow in the given histopathological image can influence the surrounding cells by:
questions.explanation:
The area marked by the arrow in the given histopathological image is Islets of Langerhans and it can influence the surrounding cells by paracrine effect.  The endocrine pancreas is in the form of numerous rounded collections of cells that are embedded within the exocrine part. These collections of polyhedral cells are called Islets of Langerhans. They appear as groups of small cells with lightly stained cytoplasm. Each islet is separated from the surrounding alveoli by a thin layer of reticular tissue and are very richly supplied with blood through a dense capillary plexus. The Islet of Langerhans is mainly composed of three types of cells as follows * α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon  * β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin  * δ or D cells- peripherally placed like α cells and secrete somatostatin and gastrin

While islet hormones maintain systemic homeostasis, they also critically regulate cells within the islet through paracrine signaling mechanisms to fine-tune cell function and survival.  In paracrine signaling, the signaling molecules released by a cell only affect target cells in close proximity to it. The densely packed nature of islet cells and blood vessels facilitates a paracrine signaling network mediated by proximity, cell contact via gap junctions, and local blood flow. Other examples of paracrine signaling include enteroendocrine cells of gastrointestinal tract.  The below image shows the different types of extracellular cell-to-cell communication mechanisms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: 10. Which of the following nerves is not involved in olfaction?
questions.explanation:
The hypoglossal nerve is not involved in olfaction. The hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) is a purely motor nerve that innervates the muscles of the tongue (except palatoglossus). It does not carry any sensory or special sensory (smell) fibers, and it has no anatomical or functional connection to the olfactory system. Therefore, it plays no role in the sense of smell. The other three cranial nerves—trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves are mixed cranial nerves and contribute to olfaction. Other options: Option A: The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), particularly its ophthalmic and maxillary divisions, is involved in olfaction indirectly. While it does not detect odors, it carries general sensory information like pain, touch, and temperature from the nasal mucosa. Trigeminal fibers can detect noxious chemicals (like ammonia and sulphur dioxide), contributing to the perception of irritation or burning, which complements the sense of smell. Option B: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) carries general sensation from the pharynx and larynx and can respond to strong irritants. Vagal nerve stimulation has been shown to modify the electrical activity of the olfactory bulb. Option C: The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) carries taste and general sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue. While it is primarily involved in gustation, it can be indirectly involved in olfaction and contribute to the overall flavour of food. Pearl PM2242: Functional components of cranial nerves

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below :
questions.explanation:
The cells marked in the above histological image are Purkinje cells.

Characteristics of Purkinje cells:

  • Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.
  • The cells are evenly spaced and are arranged in a single layer.
  • A dendrite arises from the neck of each flask-shaped cell, which passes upward to enter the molecular layer, which then branches extensively to form a dendritic tree.
  • The axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer to enter the white matter.
  • Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex.
  • The initial segment of the axon receives synaptic contacts from basket cell axons.
  • The main axon terminates in one of the cerebellar or vestibular nuclei.
  • Purkinje cells are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Pathological significance:

  • Negri bodies in rabies, are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells.
  • Loss of Purkinje cells and granule cells is seen in ataxia-telangiectasia.
  • In patients with subacute cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells. Some patients show circulating PCA­1 antibody (anti­Yo) against Purkinje cells.
  • Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia, and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

There are two methods for localization of the facial nerve trunk: 

1. Anterograde method: The facial nerve trunk is identified based on the anatomical landmarks after it exits from the stylomastoid foramen. This includes:

  • Tragal pointer/Conley's pointer - It is the inferior portion of the cartilaginous canal. The facial nerve trunk lies 1 cm deep and inferior to its tip.
  • Posterior belly of digastric - The facial nerve lies superior to the upper border of the muscle.
  • Squamotympanic fissure - It is a fissure in the temporal bone, which runs from TMJ to the tympanic cavity. The facial nerve runs through this fissure.
  • Styloid process - The facial nerve lies superficial to it.
  • Mastoid process - Upon drilling it, the nerve is identified proximally.

2. Retrograde method: The main branches of the facial nerve trunk are identified and are then traced proximally until the main tunk is identified. Some branches used for tracing the facial nerve trunk include:

  • Buccal branch - It lies in relation to the parotid gland.

questions.question: Which of the following structures prevents the upward extension of thyroid swelling through its attachment to the thyroid cartilage?
questions.explanation:
Sternothyroid and sternohyoid prevent the upward extension of the thyroid swelling through its attachment to the thyroid cartilage.

Pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid gland and is attached to the larynx. This attachment is responsible for the movement of the enlarged thyroid gland on deglutition.

The thyrohyoid membrane is a fibro-elastic ligament, which arises from the superior margin of the thyroid cartilage, and gets attached to the hyoid bone. It facilitates the upward movement of the larynx during swallowing.

questions.question: Meiosis occurs in:
questions.explanation:
Meiosis occurs in the adult ovary.

Meiosis takes place only in germ cells and results in the formation of haploid gametes. Meiosis requires two cell divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II, to reduce the number of chromosomes to the haploid number of 23.

Option C: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty. Primordial germ cells (PGCs) remain dormant in the testis until puberty. At puberty, PGCs differentiate into spermatogonial stem cells. These spermatogonial stem cells then give rise to spermatogonia which marks the beginning of spermatogenesis.

Options A and D: These are somatic cells that only undergo mitosis and not meiosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.explanation:
The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the left 6th arch artery.

During the development, the laryngeal nerves initially arise below the 6th arch artery and cross here to innervate the intrinsic muscles of the larynx. As the larynx moves cranially relative to the aortic arch arteries, the recurrent laryngeal nerves on the right and left sides are caught under the 6th arch arteries.

On the right side, the distal 6th arch artery disappears. Since there is no 5th arch artery, the right recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under the 4th arch artery which becomes the future right subclavian artery.

On the left side, the 6th arch artery persists, which develops into ductus arteriosus, which later forms ligamentum arteriosum. Due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under it and therefore, has a relatively long course.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presented with weakness of the right side of the face with the loss of pain and temperature. Pain and temperature sensation of the left leg is also lost. The lesion is most likely located at?
questions.explanation:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral pontine syndrome which occurs due to a lesion located at lateral pons.

Lateral pontine syndrome occurs due to the involvement of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery.

  • Ipsilateral manifestations include:
    • CN VII: Facial paralysis 
    • CN V: loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face.
    • Vestibular nerve or nucleus: Horizontal and vertical nystagmus, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, oscillopsia.
    • Auditory nerve or cochlear nucleus: Deafness, tinnitus.
    • Middle cerebellar peduncle: Ataxia of limb and gait.
  • Contralateral manifestations include:
    • Spinothalamic tract: Loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body.

Medial pontine syndrome occurs due to the involvement of the paramedian branch of the basilar artery.

  • Ipsilateral manifestation
    • CN VI: Diplopia(lateral rectus muscle paralysis - the affected eye looks downwards and inwards)
    • Vestibular nucleus: Nystagmus.
    • Middle cerebellar peduncle: Ataxia of limb and gait.
  • Contralateral manifestation
    • Corticobulbar and corticospinal tract: Paralysis of face, arm, and leg.
    • Medial lemniscus: loss of touch and proprioception from the body.

questions.question: A patient presented with an enlarged inguinal lymph node. The most likely primary cause is
questions.explanation:
The most likely primary cause of an enlarged inguinal lymph node is anal cancer. 

Lymphatics from the anal canal distal to the dentate line (anal margin) drains into the inguinal lymph nodes. Hence, anal cancer arising distal to dentate line can cause enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. Lymphatics proximal to the dentate line (anal canal) drains into internal iliac lymph nodes through superior rectal lymphatics.

  • Lymph nodes beside the internal iliac vein and in the hollow of the sacrum
  • External iliac lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question:
Arrange in sequence the structures involved in the direct pathway:

1. Striatum
2. Globus pallidus
3. Substantia nigra
4. Thalamus
5. Cortex
questions.explanation:
The sequence of structures involved in the direct pathway is cortex > striatum > globus pallidus > substantia nigra > thalamus.



There are five parallel circuits that connect the frontal cortex to the striatum, pallidum, substantia nigra, and thalamus. These circuits have both direct and indirect pathways. The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibit it. 

The cerebral cortex projects into the striatum. The striatum is seen projected into the pallidum and substantia nigra pars reticularis. Fibres originate from different striatal cells according to their endings in the external and internal pallidum. In the direct pathway, striatal neurones project directly to the internal pallidum.  Whereas some other fibres that arise from the neurons project to the external pallidum. This is called the indirect pathway.  

The sequence of structures involved in the indirect pathway is cortex > striatum > globus pallidus externa > subthalamic nucleus > globus pallidus interna and substantia nigra >Thalamus

The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in the indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. 

Putamen lies lateral and the internal capsule lies medial to the pallidum. It receives fibres from the striatum and subthalamic nuclei. It acts as the main output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus and superior colliculus. The substantia nigra is seen in each cerebral peduncle of the midbrain located deep to the crus cerebri. The levels of dopamine in the substantia nigra and striata are seen reduced in parkinsonism disease.



In parkinsonism disease, due to the death of neurons in substantia nigra activity of the direct pathway is reduced and the indirect pathway is increased. This results in bradykinesia in parkinsonism disease. Whereas in Huntington's disease, the activity of the indirect pathway is affected resulting in choreic involuntary movements.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the volume of the prostate in normal adult males?
questions.explanation:
The volume of the prostate in normal adult males is 20cc.

Prostate is an accessory glandular tissue embedded in the fibromuscular stroma. It usually weighs 8 grams in the young adults and its weight ranges from 40-150 grams in men aged >50 years. 

The prostate gland is situated in the lesser pelvis and surrounds the prostatic urethra which extends from bladder base to the membranous urethra. Pubic symphysis and pubic arch lie anteriorly to the prostate whereas rectourethralis and rectal ampulla lie posteriorly to it. 

The prostate has three distinct zones as follows:

Zone Structures enclosed Clinical significance
Transitional zone Urethra  Most common site for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
Central zone Ejaculatory ducts Atrophies secondary to BPH
Peripheral zone

Central and transitional zones Pre-prostatic urethra

 Most common site for prostatic carcinoma

 



The prostate is composed of 5 lobes. They are anterior, posterior, two lateral and one medial or middle lobe. 

The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae. It is an elevation found in the lower part of the bladder trigone. It is the most common site of adenoma. 

 



Microstructure of the prostate gland: 

The glandular tissue of the prostate gland is composed of many follicles with frequent internal papillae. The follicular epithelium is either a single-layered or pseudostratified columnar epithelum. These follicles open into canals, which join to form the main ducts. Small eosinophilic colloid amyloid bodies called corpora amylacea are frequently seen within a follicle. 

The prostatic ducts open into the prostatic sinus in the prostatic urethra. The ducts of the prostate follicles are lined by bilayered epithelium (basal cuboidal and apical columnar). 

The secretions of the prostate are acidic and contain acid phosphatase, amylase, prostate-specific antigen (PSA), fibrin, and zinc.

The blood supply to the prostate is by the inferior vesical, internal pudendal and middle rectal arteries. It recieves nerve supply from the inferior hypogastric plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which ligament connects medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal?
questions.explanation:
The Lisfranc ligament connects the medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal.

Lisfranc ligament is a cuneometatarsal interosseous ligament. It is the strongest ligament among the three cuneometatarsal interosseous ligaments. It passes from the lateral surface of the medial cuneiform to the adjacent angle of the second metatarsal bone. 

Deformity of this ligament can lead to instability and deformity of the tarsometatarsal joint.



Other options:
Option A: Chopart's ligament is related to both calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular joints. It is a strong Y-shaped band, having a proximal stem and 2 distal limbs.

  • The proximal limb is attached by a stem to the anterior part of the upper calcaneal surface.
  • The distal limb divides into calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular parts.


Option B: Spring ligament also known as the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament connects the sustentaculum tali to the navicular. It ties the calcaneus to the navicular and maintains the medial longitudinal arch of the foot. It is made up of the superomedial calcaneonavicular portion and the inferior calcaneonavicular portion.



Option D: Deltoid ligament also called the medial collateral ligament is attached to the apex, anterior and posterior borders of the medial malleolus. It has 2 layers, superficial and deep:

  • The superficial layer consists of tibionavicular fibres anteriorly, tibiocalcaneal fibres in the middle, and superficial posterior tibiotalar fibres posteriorly.
  • Deep layer consists of anterior tibiotalar fibres, tibiocalcaneal in the middle and deep posterior tibiotalar posteriorly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Fibres of the given structure originate from ?
questions.explanation:
The given structure is the fornix and its fibres arise from the hippocampus. 

The fornix is a part of the connecting pathways of the limbic system. It arises from the hippocampus which wraps around the thalamus and ends in the mammillary body. It connects the hippocampus with distal brain sites. 

The fornix has two types of fibres:

  • Association fibres: They connect the various cortical regions within the same hemisphere 
  • Commissural fibres: They connect the corresponding regions of two hemispheres. It is seen in the hippocampal commissure of the fornix. 

The blood supply of fornix is by the anterior communicating artery which arises from the anterior cerebral artery. 

The limbic system is a group of structures seen between the cerebral cortex and the hypothalamus. It is involved in emotional and motivation activity, learning, and memory. 



Other options:

Option A: Amygdala is a part of the limbic system that consists of lateral, central and basal nuclei. It can Influence the body's response to enviromnental changes. In a fearful situation it can change the heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate etc. 

Option C: Caudate nucleus is a C-shaped mass of grey matter. It is divided into a head, body, and tail. Degeneration of the caudate nucleus is seen in Huntington's disease.

questions.question: Which structure is supplied by the nerve causing this elevation?
questions.explanation:
Risorius is supplied by the facial nerve which causes the elevation marked. The image shows the floor of the fourth ventricle and the facial colliculus is marked. 

The fourth ventricle is located between the brainstem and the cerebellum. The rhomboid fossa is a diamond-shaped depression seen on the floor of the fourth ventricle. The superior and the inferior part of the floor is triangular in shape. It is divided by a longitudinal median sulcus into two halves. Each half is again divided into the medial and lateral regions.

The facial colliculus is present in the superior part, which presents as a small elevation produced by the root of the facial nerve winding around the nucleus of the abducens nerve.  Columns are formed by groups of facial neurones, which innervate individual muscles and give branches of the facial nerve. Dorsal neurones innervate muscles in the scalp and upper face and ventral neurons supply the lower facial musculature. 

Risorius falls under the buccolabial muscle group and act as the elevator, retractor and evertor of the upper lip. Some of its peripheral attachments are the zygomatic arch, parotid fascia and fascia over the mastoid process. It is involved in actions like grinning and laughing and is innervated by the buccal branches of the facial nerve.



Other options:

Option A: Lateral rectus is an extraocular muscle that arises from the lateral part of the common tendinous ring. It is innervated by the abducens nerve. 

Option B: Superior oblique is an extraocular muscle that arises from the body of the sphenoid. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve. 

Option D: Levator palpebrae superiors is an extraocular muscle that arises from the lesser wing of sphenoid. It is innervated by the oculomotor nerve.

Mental is not a branch of the facial artery but the branch of the maxillary artery in the face.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structures passing via jugular foramen has a separate canal?
questions.explanation:
The glossopharyngeal nerve passing through the jugular foramen has a separate canal.

 The jugular foramen is formed by the occipital bone and the petrous part of the temporal bone. The spinal accessory nerve and vagus nerve also pass through this foramen.

The glossopharyngeal nerve leaves the skull through the anteromedial part of the jugular foramen in a separate dural sheath.

The branches of the nerve are tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar and lingual branches.

Infection, malignancy and postoperative inflammation of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa will cause referred pain in the ear. This is conducted through the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are:

  • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
  • All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve)

 Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc.

The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of the posterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate etc. 

The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing, phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx. 

Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include:

  • Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
  • By assessing the strength of the cough

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the nerve supply of the structure marked in the image?
questions.explanation:
The median nerve supplies the 1st lumbrical which is marked. 

There are four lumbrical muscles. They originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus. It passes to the radial side of the corresponding fingers and is inserted into the dorsal digital expansion of the extensor digitorum.

The action of lumbricals is flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joint and extension of interphalangeal joints. 

Lumbricals can be tested only along with interosseous muscle. The examiner will hold the metacarpophalangeal joint of the index finger in hyperextension. Then the patient is asked to extend the proximal interphalangeal joint against resistance. The test is repeated on other fingers as well.

The median nerve innervates the first and second lumbricals. The deep terminal branch of the ulnar nerve innervates the third and the fourth. 



The median nerve is formed by the union of the lateral root (C6, 7) from the lateral cord, and the medial root (C8, T1) from the medial cord.

On the hand, it is seen proximal to the flexor retinaculum and lateral to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis. It also lies between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus.

Its cutaneous supply in hand is as follows: 

  • Lateral 2/3rd of the palm by superficial cutaneous branch
  • Lateral 3½ fingers (palmar aspect and dorsal aspect of nailbeds) by palmar digital nerves


The muscles supplied by the median nerve in the hand are flexor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis

The median nerve sometimes gets compressed under the fibro-osseous tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum leading to carpal tunnel syndrome. 

Pen test is used to test the median nerve in the hand. It tests the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.  The hand must remain flat with the palm facing upwards. A pen is held above the palm and the patient is asked to touch the pen with his thumb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A child lacks thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Defective development of which of the following structures is likely to be the cause?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. Defective development of the third pharyngeal pouch marked as 3 causes this condition.

A child with DiGeorge syndrome lacks thymus and inferior parathyroid glands due to defective development of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch. The child can also lack superior parathyroid glands, due to defective development of the 4th pharyngeal pouch. It is caused by chromosome 22q deletion and is characterized by the following (Mnemonic: CATCH-22)

  • Cleft palate
  • Abnormal facies
  • Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency and recurrent infections
  • Cardiac defects
  • Hypocalcemia, secondary to parathyroid aplasia. 

Derivatives of the Pharyngeal Pouches

1st Pouch

  • Tympanic cavity (middle ear cavity)
  • Auditory tube (eustachian tube) 

2nd Pouch

  • Palatine tonsils
  • Tonsillar fossa

3rd Pouch

  • Inferior parathyroid glands 
  • Thymus

4th Pouch

  • Superior parathyroid glands 
  • Ultimobranchial body - gives rise to parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland

 



The medulla of the thymus has Hassall’s corpuscles. They are small rounded structures formed from whorls of medullary epithelial cells with a central partially keratinized core appearing as an eosinophilic-staining mass.

In holocrine secretions, the secretory cells themselves are disintegrated as part of their terminal differentiation. Afterwhich, the terminally differentiated cells filled with lipid products are released. The sebaceous gland and hair follicles are examples.

questions.question: Superior gluteal nerve supplies all of the following structures except:
questions.explanation:
All of the structures except pyriformis are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. Pyriformis is supplied by the nerve to the piriformis. 

The dorsal branches of the L4, L5, and S1 rami give rise to the superior gluteal nerve. It is accompanied by superior gluteal vessels. This nerve leaves the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis and divides into superior and inferior branches. It supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae.

The dorsal branches of the S1 and S2 rami give rise to the nerve to the piriformis. 

Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis on the femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject to stand on one limb. If the ipsilateral abductors are normal, the pelvis remains in a horizontal position. If the ipsilateral abductors are weak, then the pelvis tilts towards the opposite (unsupported) side. This is called positive Trendelenburg’s sign.

The sartorius muscle is known as the tailor muscle and is also the longest muscle in the body. The word "sartorius" is derived from the Latin word sartor, which translates to tailor, due to the way the individual will position one's leg while working.

Origin: Anterior superior iliac spine and the upper half of the notch below it.

Insertion: Into the superior aspect of the medial surface of the tibial shaft near the tibial tuberosity (joins aponeurosis of gracilis and semitendinosus to form pes anserinus).

Option C: Gracilis is involved in adduction at the hip and flexion and medial rotation at the knee.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The rupture of penile urethra does not cause extravasation of blood into which of the following spaces?
questions.explanation:
Rupture of the penile urethra causes extravasation of blood into the superficial perineal pouch, scrotum, penis, and then up to the lower anterior abdominal wall.

The superficial perineal pouch is a compartment of the perineum enclosed by the membranous layer of the perineal fascia that surrounds the scrotum or labia and penis or clitoris.

Anteriorly, the membranous layer of perineal fascia is continuous over the pubic symphysis and pubic bones. It is later continuous with the membranous layer of the anterior abdominal wall.  Thus, the fluid that accumulates in the perineal pouch extends to the lower anterior abdomen.

In the lower lateral abdominal wall, the abdominal fascia is attached to the deep fascia of the thigh, inferior to the inguinal ligament. Thus, on trauma at the penile urethra, urine does not extravasate into the anterior thigh.

The superficial perineal pouch is closed posteriorly by attaching the membranous layer of superficial fascia to the posterior margin of the urogenital diaphragm. Thus, commonly there is no extravasation into the deep perineal pouch and the ischiorectal fossa.

Also, the membranous layer of superficial fascia attaches to the ischiopubic rami and forms the lateral borders of the urogenital triangle. Thus, the urine does not extravasate to the thigh.

But, the ischiorectal fossa would be a better answer because of the following reasons:

  1. Bulbourethral glands that lie in the deep perineal space open their ducts into the spongy urethra, which is related to the superficial perineal space. Also, the muscles surrounding these glands were recently found to be a continuation of the deep transverse perinei and tail of the external urethral sphincter, both of which are components of the deep perineal space. Injury to the penile urethra can damage bulbourethral glands' ducts, which can lead to damage to the above-mentioned structures and may cause extravasation of urine into the deep perineal space. 
  2. Previously, the perineal membrane was thought to be a triangular membrane. However, recent studies show that it is contiguous anteriorly with the structures that support the urethra. Posteriorly, it is related to the support of the perineal body and lateral vaginal wall. So damage to the urethra might damage the anterior part of the perineal membrane which can make way for extravasation of blood into the deep perineal space. 
  3. Deep perineal pouch: It was believed initially that the urogenital diaphragm was formed by 3 layers: An inferior fascia (also called the perineal membrane), deep perineal space, and a superior fascia. The superior fascia formed the inferior border of the ischioanal fossa. The Colles fascia also separates the perineal membrane from the ischioanal fossa. So, extravasation of blood into the deep perineal space is possible but extravasation into the ischioanal fossa due to penile urethral injury is highly unlikely. Recent studies have shown that this might be a slightly more complex structure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which nerve is blocked when local anesthesia is given below the inguinal ligament during femoral vein catheterization?
questions.explanation:
Genitofemoral nerve is blocked when the local anesthetic is given below the inguinal ligament during femoral vein catheterization. 

The genitofemoral nerve originates from the L1 and L2 ventral rami. It divides into the genital and femoral branches after crossing behind the ureter.

The genital branch enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring and accompanies the spermatic cord or round ligament. It exits the superficial inguinal ring and supplies the cremaster muscle and skin of the external genitalia.

The femoral branch descends lateral to the external iliac artery to pass behind the inguinal ligament and enter the femoral sheath lateral to the femoral artery. It pierces the anterior wall of the femoral sheath and fascia lata and supplies them.

The genitofemoral nerve gives sensory supply to the anteromedial thigh via the femoral branch. The genital branch supplies skin of the scrotum in males and mons pubis and labium majus in females. The genitofemoral nerve also innervates the cremaster muscle via the genital branch and is responsible for the cremasteric reflex.

The image given below shows nerves related to the inguinal region:



Other options:

Option A: Femoral nerve arises from the posterior division of ventral rami of L2-L4 spinal segments on the posterior abdominal wall. It enters the femoral triangle by passing under the inguinal ligament. In the femoral triangle, it lies lateral to the femoral artery and outside the femoral sheath. Later, it is divided into anterior and posterior branches by the lateral circumflex femoral artery.

Option C: Lateral cutaneous nerve (a.k.a lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) of the thigh is most commonly injured at the site where it leaves the pelvis. An injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh leads to pain and paresthesia over the anterolateral region of the thigh, a condition called meralgia paresthetica.

Option D: Ilioinguinal nerve is most commonly injured within the inguinal canal in open hernia repair due to traction or thermal injury. Injury causes loss of sensation in the root of the penis and adjacent part of the scrotum.

questions.question: Identify the nerve passing around the marked structure.
questions.explanation:
The structure marked in the given image is the neck of fibula. The nerve passing around the neck of fibula is the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve).

The common peroneal nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the ventral rami of L4, L5, S1, and S2. The sciatic nerve divides into the tibial nerve and the common fibular nerve.

The common fibular nerve runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

Superficial fibular nerve:

Motor innervation: 

  • Peroneus longus
  • Peroneus brevis

Sensory innervation: 

  • Lateral aspect of the lower leg
  • Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital webspace

Deep fibular nerve:

Motor innervation:

  • Extensor digitorum longus
  • Extensor hallucis longus
  • Tibialis anterior
  • Peroneus tertius

Sensory innervation:

  • The first interdigital space


The common peroneal nerve is more prone to injury as it lies superficial at the level of the lateral aspect of the neck of the fibula. Injury results in foot drop (which causes high-stepping gait), loss of eversion of the foot, and sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot.

questions.question: Bleeding as shown in the image is due to which of the following vessels?
questions.explanation:
The image showing a bleed over the arachnoid layer but under the dura is suggestive of a subdural hemorrhage. Most commonly, it results from the shearing of cortical bridging veins.  

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid layers of the meninges. The causes of SDH include

  • anticoagulants, antiplatelets
  • alcohol abuse
  • battered baby syndrome. 

Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice.

Middle meningeal artery rupture would result in an extradural hemorrhage.

Lenticulostriate artery would lead to an intraparenchymal hemorrhage.



Vertebral artery dissection leads to subarachnoid hemorrhage or sometimes intraparenchymal hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question:
Which of the following statements are true about the internal capsule?
  1. Charcot's artery supplies the posterior limb.
  2. Retrolenticular part of the internal capsule contains optic radiation.
  3. Anterior limb of the capsule contains corticospinal tract fibers of the upper limb and face.
  4. Internal capsule has projection fibers.
questions.explanation:
Statements 1, 2, and 4 are true about the internal capsule.

The charcot’s artery of hemorrhage is a larger lenticulostriate or lateral striate artery. Lateral striate arteries supply the anterior limb, genu and the posterior limb of the internal capsule. These arteries are also commonly involved in ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes.

The retrolentiform part of the internal capsule carries fibers mainly from optic radiation. A lesion here produces homonymous hemianopia, superior quadrantanopia, or inferior quadrantanopia.

The anterior limb of the internal capsule carries fronto-pontine fibers. A lesion here produces confusion, impaired attention, agitation, and dysarthria.

The posterior limb of the internal capsule carries cortico-spinal motor fibers in the anterior part and the lesion here produces contralateral hemiparesis. The posterior part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule carries sensory fibers and lesions here may produce contralateral hemi-sensory deficits.

The internal capsule predominantly contains projection fibers, not commissural fibers. Projection fibers are the fibers that project from higher to lower centers or vice versa in CNS.

questions.question: Identify the incorrect statement regarding the marked structure.
options: It is the meeting point of frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones.

questions.correct_answer: Accessory middle meningeal artery lies under this structure.
questions.explanation:
The structure marked in the image is the pterion. The incorrect statement is statement 3, which is the accessory middle meningeal artery lies under this structure.

The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

  1. Frontal bone
  2. Squamous part of the temporal bone
  3. Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
  4. Parietal bone

It is located approximately 4 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch. 



 

The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and the lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin, and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery, leading to extradural hematoma.

The pterion also corresponds to the site of the anterolateral (sphenoidal) fontanelle of the neonatal skull, which closes in the third month after birth.



 

The accessory meningeal artery may be a branch of the middle meningeal artery or might arise directly from the maxillary artery. It reaches the cranium via the foramen ovale and distributes principally in the extracranial region. It is distributed over the medial and lateral pterygoids, tensor veli palatini, greater wing and pterygoid processes of the sphenoid bone, mandibular nerve, and the otic ganglion. So, it supplies the trigeminal ganglion, dura mater and bone. But in some people, it may be replaced by small separate arteries.

questions.question:
Which of the following muscles form the pelvic diaphragm?

A. Iliococcygeus
B. Pubococcygeus
C. Obturator internus
D. Deep transverse perinei
questions.explanation:
Iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus are parts of the pelvic diaphragm, which is also known as the levator ani.

The levator ani muscle is a complex unit that consists of 3 muscle components:

  • Pubococcygeus
    • Pubovaginalis - elevates the urethra and hence contributes to urinary continence
    • Puboperinealis - draws the perineal body towards the pubic symphysis
    • Puboanalis - elevates the anus and keeps the urogenital hiatus narrowed
  • Puborectalis
  • Iliococcygeus

Levator ani muscles are the most important muscles in the pelvic floor and maintain a constant state of contraction. They provide a stable floor and support the weight of the abdominopelvic contents against intra-abdominal forces. Weakening of levator ani and pelvic fascia from stretching or tearing during childbirth, may decrease support for the vagina, bladder, uterus, or rectum or alter the position of the neck of the bladder and urethra.

Other options: 

The obturator internus forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa and is not a part of the levator ani.

The deep transverse perineal muscle is the content of the deep perineal space and contributes to the formation of the perineal body.
